[[On the Dial]] It takes Thursday because Thursday's arm belongs to the Priest-Teacher, and Eleusis produced antiquity's own template for that very office: the Hierophant, 'the one who shows the sacred,' a title held hereditarily by the Eumolpidae clan for two thousand years — the word history has borrowed ever since for any priest of a mystery. Its arm stands at the yellow 12h top, in noon's own harvest-gold, Demeter's gift before it is ever bread.

[[The Lesson]] The arm pairs Generosity with Excess under the Priest-Teacher, and no mystery cult of the ancient world gave more freely: the kykeon cup was offered to any Greek-speaker who walked the Sacred Way from Athens to Eleusis and had not killed — slave beside citizen, woman beside man, on the same processional road. Excess is the same rite profaned: in 415 BCE Alcibiades and his circle were accused of performing the Mysteries as a drunken party trick outside the sanctuary, the scandal that drove them into exile — the one crime this generosity could never forgive.

variants.hexa_primary: On the pigment hexagram the Jupiter body wears yellow, a painter's primary — and the wheat sheaf itself already wears it, threshed and given rather than kept. Demeter's oldest title, Sito, 'she of the grain,' names the same color the wheel does before either one was ever asked to.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light world the same noon arm turns pure green (#00DC00), one of the three primary beams that sum to white. The Telesterion held thousands of initiates under one roof for a single shared rite, no separate fire kept for any one of them alone — a green built from joined beams reads the same way: no single lamp, one witnessed hall.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass the Eleusinian Mysteries keep their noon arm, now alb ivory (#EDEDE0) — the estate of the Priest, the Bell for its object — and the Hierophant, 'the one who shows the sacred,' already held that very office for two thousand years before the word was ever borrowed for anyone else's priesthood.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel noon is Childhood, spring green (#7CE577) — and the epopteia, the beholding, the moment initiates were finally shown the light none could ever describe again, is Childhood's own wonder given back to grown initiates: a first sight, kept sacred by never being repeated in words.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross the Jupiter body takes the summer arm, the year's noon. The Mysteries' own rite fell in autumn, but the Attic wheat harvest itself does not wait that long — cut and threshed in the weeks either side of the solstice, months before Demeter's own festival, this arm keeps the grain's actual season even though her rite keeps a later one.
variants.trio: On the Trinity pointer the Jupiter body carries the Faith arm itself, bright yellow, guarding the day's height from 8h to 16h beside Saturn. Faith here is the initiate's own word for it: Cicero, who had walked the Sacred Way himself, wrote that the rites taught a mortal 'not only to live with joy, but to die with a better hope' — trust professed once, at the one initiation an entire city kept silent about forever after.

jupiter.name: Eleusinian Mysteries

saturn.name: Voodoo
saturn.base:
[[The Figure]] Vodou was born in Haiti when West African religion survived the slave ships, wearing Catholic saints as masks: one creator, Bondye, served through the lwa, spirits who ride their people in ceremony, and the ancestors.

[[On the Dial]] It rules Saturday through Baron Samedi - 'Baron Saturday' - keeper of the crossroads and the dead, at home on Saturn's green arm at hour 8, the Farmer's arm: the Ghede govern graves and fertility alike.

[[The Lesson]] The arm's Patience is the ancestor-faith itself, debts honored over generations; its Envy is the sorcery Vodou is slandered with and its ethics condemn. Green Renewal is its truth: nothing sprouts that was not buried.

variants.hexa_primary: On the pigment hexagram the Saturn body wears green, the painter's mix of yellow and blue - growth out of dark ground. Pigment is Vodou's own medium: veve traced in cornmeal and ash on the temple floor, color poured onto earth to open a way. This green is graveyard grass, life fed by the dead.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the world of light the arm cools from green to cyan (#00DDDD), the pale sky just before sunrise. There is a quiet justice in that: a faith of the enslaved, long dismissed as darkness, wears the dawn's own color in the brighter wheel. Cyan is the Ghede's paradox made visible - out of the tomb, the first light of morning.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass Vodou keeps its dawn arm, now field green (#3E8914) — the estate of the Farmer, the Plough for its object — and Baron Samedi, Baron Saturday, already governs graves and fertility together: the Ghede's whole office is proof that nothing sprouts that was not first buried.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel dawn is Birth, predawn mist (#8FA8C8) — and an ancestor-faith built on debts honored over generations finds its truest hour here: the dead are kept close precisely so that Birth, when it comes, arrives already known and already welcomed.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross the Saturn body at hour 8 flanks the dawn arm - the spring equinox side, shared with the Moon. Spring is this faith's deepest teaching made season: the Ghede who rule the grave rule fertility too, and nothing sprouts that was not first buried. Dawn out of the cemetery is Vodou's whole hope.
variants.trio: On the Trinity pointer the Saturn body stands on the Faith arm, bright yellow, guarding 8h to 16h beside Jupiter. Vodou's faith is service, sevis lwa - a reciprocal bond: feed the spirits and they hold your world steady. Even the Baron, joking at death's gate, is trusted utterly to open it.

sun.name: Mithraism (Sol Invictus)
sun.base:
[[The Figure]] Mithraism was Rome's best-kept secret: a mystery religion of soldiers, merchants and customs officers that spread from Britain to the Euphrates between the first and fourth centuries, worshipping in windowless cave-temples called mithraea. Its whole architecture was the week's: seven grades of initiation, each under one of the seven planets — Corax the Raven under Mercury, Nymphus the Bridegroom under Venus, Miles the Soldier under Mars, Leo the Lion under Jupiter, Perses the Persian under the Moon, Heliodromus the Sun-Runner under the Sun, Pater the Father under Saturn. A Mithraist did not merely keep the planetary week; he climbed it.

[[On the Dial]] It guards Sunday by the shortest possible chain of title: this IS the cult of dies Solis. In 274 Aurelian made Sol Invictus, the Unconquered Sun, the empire's official god; in 321 Constantine decreed rest on 'the venerable day of the Sun' — the very Sunday this dial still keeps. And the tauroctony itself is a star map: bull Taurus, dog Canis, serpent Hydra, raven Corvus, scorpion Scorpius — the constellations strung along the celestial equator, the turning sky mastered at a stroke. The white-gold CENTER, the source the six colors decompose from, is exactly where Rome put its unconquered source of light.

[[The Lesson]] Senators crawled blindfolded through initiation as Ravens and served at table long before rising toward Pater, while the radiate crown of Sol became the very costume emperors reached for when Pride wanted one — so the center pairs Humility against Pride, and even Sol does not command Mithras but shakes his hand, the dexiosis. Yet the center is DOUBLE, two virtues, two vices, two moods in one seat, and the mysteries drilled that doubleness into every initiate: whoever rose to Pater had first crawled as a Corax and served the banquet — the king in the cult was its former servant, on purpose. Justice was the grade ladder itself, the same seven steps for senator and slave; Servility its corruption, serving rank instead of light. Sol INVICTUS names the mood pair outright: the Unconquered Sun is Glory precisely because the Awe never holds it.

variants.hexa_primary: On the paint hexa Mithraism holds the unmixable white-gold center, and its founding image agrees: Mithras petrogenitus, born out of solid rock with the torch already lit. Light out of stone — given from elsewhere, never mixed on a palette — is the paint wheel's doctrine of the center told as a nativity.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light world six beams sum to white at the hub, and the cult built exactly that room: a mithraeum had no windows, so the only sun in the cave was the one the mysteries carried in — Sol's radiate face over the bull, emission in the dark, white light assembled where no daylight reaches.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass Mithraism keeps its noon-center arm, now royal gold (#F0C420) — the estate of the King, the Crown for its object — and Rome had already crowned this exact light: Aurelian's Sol Invictus, the Unconquered Sun, wearing the radiate crown emperors later reached for whenever Pride wanted one.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel noon is Youth, sun-yellow (#FFE800) — and the cult kept a uniformed office for precisely this hour: Heliodromus, the Sun-Runner, sixth of the seven grades, whose whole duty was to walk the sun's road at its freshest and fastest, before any grade's slower wisdom set in.
variants.cross: The seasons cross points its four arms at solstices and equinoxes — and that is the tauroctony's deepest reading: bull Taurus and scorpion Scorpius are the old equinoctial pair, and the slaying has been read as the precession itself, the spring point wrestled out of Taurus. A god whose slaying of the bull is itself the wheel of the year in motion belongs naturally at the crossing where the year's four hinges meet.
variants.trio: On the Trinity pointer the Sun keeps the center and the yellow arm of Faith rises vertically from it — Mithraism's native virtue, sworn rather than felt: initiates bound themselves by sacramentum, the soldier's oath, and the handshake of Mithras and Sol above the bull is Roman fides cast in bronze. Faith as a contract kept in the dark and paid at dawn, with Hope at 4h and Love at 20h fanning from the same disc.

faces.ruler:
Mithraism is the Ruler face — Rome's best-kept secret, a mystery religion of soldiers and merchants worshipping in windowless cave-temples, its whole architecture built on seven grades of initiation, one for each planet.

Its virtue is Justice, the same seven-grade ladder climbed by senator and slave alike, no rank exempted from the same steps — but that ladder is stalked by Pride, the radiate crown of Sol becoming exactly the costume emperors reached for when they wanted to look unconquerable rather than earn it. Its mood is Glory, Sol Invictus itself, the Unconquered Sun blazing over the cave precisely because no eclipse ever holds it for long.
faces.servant:
Corax is the Servant face — the Raven, the first and lowest of the seven Mithraic grades, standing in for every initiate before he has climbed a single rung toward Pater.

Its virtue is Humility, the plain fact the cult built into its own ranks on purpose — that whoever would rise to Pater first crawled as a Corax and served the banquet — while Servility is the grade gone wrong, rank served instead of the light the rank exists to carry toward. Its mood is Awe, the initiate's own light kept deliberately low at the cave's foot — and Glory is the same figure's whole future, climbing grade by grade toward the seat now serving him his cup.

venus.name: Babylonian religion (Babylon)
venus.base:
[[The Figure]] Babylon's faith made the planets gods and the gods mathematics: its priests watched Venus from ziggurat tops, pressed her risings into clay, and named the seven days after the seven wanderers - the very week this clock still keeps was Babylon's invention.

[[On the Dial]] It guards Friday by identity, not analogy: Ishtar IS Venus, morning and evening star, and Friday is Venus' day in every tongue that kept the planetary week. The red 20h arm, Passion's hour, is her exact address - the evening star lighting the first hour of the night.

[[The Lesson]] The arm pairs Love with Jealousy, and no goddess carried both more openly: goddess of love AND war in one body, who, refused by Gilgamesh, loosed the Bull of Heaven on his city. The Artist shares her arm - and Babylon's artists answered her with the most beautiful bricks ever fired.

variants.hexa_primary: On the paint hexa Babylon wears the deep red of Venus' 20h arm as pigment - kiln-fired, like the city itself: glazed brick reds and golds burned permanent in the Ishtar Gate. Love as a material you can build walls from, jealousy as the same fire left untended.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light world the red arm becomes emission - and Ishtar was always light first: the evening star, the one lamp lit before all others in the darkening sky. Her star glows copper against lapis night exactly as Venus does at dusk.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass Ishtar keeps her 18h arm, now iron-blood crimson (#A02020) — the estate of the Soldier, the Sword for its object — and no goddess needs less persuading: she was already war and love in one body, and the Bull of Heaven loosed on Gilgamesh's city after his refusal proves Love's Jealousy could field an actual army.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel that arm is the Elder, ember (#FF6A3C) — banked fire over centuries of watching, and it suits the priests who tracked her risings from ziggurat tops for generations: a light young at every dawn, but read, over such long study, with an Elder's patience.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross Venus' body shares the autumn arm with Mars - love and war side by side, which for Babylon is no pairing at all but one goddess: Ishtar owned both. Autumn suits her too - the harvest festivals when the evening star stood longest over the city.
variants.trio: On the Trinity pointer her body stands on the red arm of Love, paired with Mars - and Babylon would call that arm simply 'Ishtar', love and war in one body, guarding the night third where the evening star reigns. Love as the theology of the first hour of darkness.

sun.base:
[[The Figure]] Ra is not a god who rules the sun; he is the sun. Every day he crosses the sky in the Mandjet, the day barque, growing old as the light reddens; every night he dies into the Duat aboard the night barque and fights his way through the serpent-haunted dark to be reborn at dawn. Three thousand years of Egyptian faith turned on that circuit — temples faced his risings, pharaohs ruled as his sons, and the other gods took their greatness by joining their names to his.

[[On the Dial]] He belongs to Sunday because Sunday is his in the oldest sense: the planetary week names this day for the Sun, and no pantheon fused sun, king and temple more completely than Egypt. On this dial the Sun takes no arm at all — it holds the white-gold center, the source the six arm colors decompose from — and Egypt anticipated exactly that geometry: Amun-Ra, Ra-Horakhty, Atum-Ra — every great god was some hue of him, flowing into and out of the one disc the way the arms flow from the hub.

[[The Lesson]] Kings called themselves sons of Ra, yet every heart, royal or common, ended on the scales against the feather of Ma'at — so the center pairs Humility with Pride, the one axis whose cure comes not from across the dial but from itself. And that center is DOUBLE, two virtues, two vices, two moods in one seat, which is simply Ra's day written as doctrine: the day barque in Glory, the night barque through the Duat in Awe, one god in two boats. His Justice is Ma'at riding at the prow, the feather every heart is weighed against, pharaoh's included; his servant face is the oarsman of his own route, aging by dusk to be reborn by dawn, and Servility is that oarsman forgetting the route is sacred. Humility answers Pride, Justice straightens Servility — the cycle heals itself nightly.

variants.hexa_primary: On the paint hexa Ra takes no arm: he holds the white-gold center, the source from which all six pigment arms take their color. Egypt drew him the same way — Amun-Ra, Ra-Horakhty, every god a hue of the one disc — and no hour belongs to him because his barque is under way through all twenty-four.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette nothing moves for Ra — the center stays white-gold, and the reading only sharpens: the disc above the falcon's brow is not a painted surface but emission itself, Newton's white beam an instant before the prism breaks it into red, green and blue — Ra at dawn pouring out every color the day will spend.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass the falcon-headed Ra takes the noon arm robed in royal gold (#F0C420) — the Walk of the King, the Crown his object — and no seat needs less argument: every pharaoh already called himself Ra's son, and the striped headdress beneath his sun-disc was a crown before it was a costume. 'By me kings reign' could have been carved at Karnak as easily as in Proverbs; the god who crosses the sky each day simply steps onto the arm built for the throne he already keeps.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel the noon arm belongs to Youth, and Ra wears the wheel's own sun-yellow (#FFE800) — a fitting recursion for a god who is reborn every single dawn and never actually grows old, dying each dusk only to rise young again each morning. Three thousand years of temples faced this risen, ever-young light; the Ages wheel simply names what the Mandjet already performed daily.
variants.cross: On the cross the arms point at the year's hinges, and Ra holds the top arm at 12h, yellow for Summer, sharing it with Jupiter — a pairing Egypt made literal: Jupiter's day belongs to Amun, and the two were fused as Amun-Ra, king of gods and sun in one name. The summer solstice was Ra's own hinge as well, Sirius rising beside it to call the flood and open the Egyptian year.
variants.trio: The Trinity returns Ra to the white-gold center with three arms around him — Faith's yellow, Love's red, Hope's blue, the painter's three primaries — and their thirds retell his voyage: Faith holds 8h–16h, the day barque's high crossing; Love takes 16h–24h, the western descent where Hathor, lady of the west, receives the aging sun; Hope keeps 0h–8h, the night passage through the Duat whose whole meaning is the certainty of dawn.

faces.ruler:
Ra is the Ruler face because Ra is not a god who rules the sun; he is the sun — three thousand years of Egyptian faith turned on his daily circuit, temples facing his risings, pharaohs ruling as his sons.

His virtue is Justice, Ma'at herself riding at the prow of the day barque, the feather every heart is weighed against, pharaoh's included — but that same authority is stalked by Pride, the son of Ra forgetting he is only weighed like everyone else. His mood is Glory, the Mandjet under full sail at noon, the god at the height of his daily strength before the long descent into dusk begins.
faces.servant:
Afu-Ra is the Servant face — "the flesh of Ra," the god's own aged, ram-headed night form, not a rival but the same Ra after the sun has set, towed rather than rowing.

In the myth he crosses the Duat ram-horned, his fire dimmed to an ember behind curved horns, while the serpent Apophis strikes at the barque's prow and is driven back by spears.

His virtue is Humility, the same god who ruled at noon reduced to cargo in his own boat, fighting to be reborn rather than commanding the day outright — and Servility is the failure the myth warns against, the oarsman forgetting that this humbling voyage is sacred and not mere transit. His mood is Awe, the night barque's whole ordeal — and Glory is simply tomorrow's dawn, the same god surfacing at the eastern horizon exactly on schedule.

moon.base:
[[The Figure]] Khonsu is "the traveller" — the moon god of Thebes who crosses the night sky as the moon itself, son of Amun and Mut in the great Theban triad. His name comes from the verb to cross: he is the wanderer whose road is the dark, and because the moon was Egypt's first calendar he is also a reckoner of time, the god who counts out the months and measures the lifespans of kings.

[[On the Dial]] On the dial he keeps Monday, the Moon's day, riding the deep blue arm at 4h — Calm, the hour before dawn, the last and stillest watch of his nightly crossing. Blue is moonlight's own temperature, and no god earned it more literally: while Ra dies each dusk and sails the underworld, it is Khonsu who holds the visible sky, the lamp of the world between sunset and sunrise. Silver, the Moon's metal at the dial's bottom tip, is his by the same right.

[[The Lesson]] Egypt gave him a paradox before it gave him a doctrine: bound mummiform like the dead, a child crowned with the moon whole yet carrying the crook and flail of kingship — eternity's regalia worn by a wrapped body. That paradox is exactly his two faces, Serenity against Fear. The oldest texts knew Khonsu fierce — a devourer in the Pyramid Texts' hymns — but Thebes came to know him as the great healer whose statue was sent abroad to cure a foreign princess: the night accepted becomes medicine, the night dreaded becomes terror. The Physician's arm fits no god better. And his cure stands straight across the dial at 16h: Montu, the falcon war god on Mars' orange arm, whose Courage cures the Moon's Fear — while Khonsu's Serenity, in return, is the cool hand that quells Montu's Wrath.

variants.hexa_primary: The home post: the 04h arm in deep pigment blue (#002FFF), Calm, the hour before dawn. Khonsu rides one arm below the sunrise line, on the last stretch of his crossing, and the paint reads like Egypt's own night pigment — the ground lapis the texts gave the gods for hair.
variants.hexa_secondary: The prism wheel keeps him at 04h and sharpens the blue to #0040FF — the pure primary, Calm read as light instead of paint. It suits him best of all the arms: the moon makes no color of its own, it only carries the sun's light across the dark, and Khonsu's electric blue is exactly that — borrowed radiance, delivered nightly.
variants.octa_primary: The 'traveller' god settles onto the deep-night arm in lamplit ink blue (#1F5FA8), the Walk of the Scholar and his Book — a seat Khonsu earns outright, since the moon was Egypt's first calendar and he its reckoner, the god who counted out months and measured the lifespans of kings. The healer who cured a foreign princess by his priests' own written rites now sits where the deep-night hours belong to study rather than fear.
variants.octa_secondary: On the Ages wheel the same deep-night arm turns moonlight silver (#C8D7F0) — the Age of the Unborn, ancestors and the not-yet-born held in one hue. Khonsu, wrapped mummiform like the dead yet crowned with the crook and flail of eternity, was always a god who belonged as much to what has not happened as to what already has; the silver simply names the space he was already standing in.
variants.cross: The cross is the seasons palette: his arm at dial 6h points at the spring equinox, colored spring green, and he shares it with Osiris. Moon god and grain god on one spoke is Egypt's whole calendar in miniature — Khonsu counts the months, Osiris dies and sprouts to count the years, and the equinox dawn belongs to both: the night's traveller handing the sky to the season of returning life.
variants.trio: The Trinity keeps Khonsu at his 04h post but renames the watch: the blue arm (#002FFF) now stands for Hope, and he shares it with Thoth — Egypt's two moon-touched gods together, the reckoner beside the traveller. The arm guards the morning third from 0h to 8h, and no one holds better title to it: Khonsu has proven on every crossing since Egypt began that the dark ends and the dawn arrives.

mars.base:
[[The Figure]] Montu is the falcon-headed war god of Thebes — the raised arm of Egypt's armies. Before Amun rose to rule the city, Montu WAS Thebes: four temples ringed his ground at Karnak, Armant, Medamud and Tod, and the Middle Kingdom's warrior kings wore his name as their own — Mentuhotep, "Montu is satisfied." When Egypt wanted to say a pharaoh fought perfectly, this god's name was the whole sentence: Thutmose III was praised as a Montu on the battlefield, and Ramses II at Kadesh raged "like Montu, lord of Thebes."

[[On the Dial]] He stands on Tuesday because he is Egypt's exact word for the red planet: dies Martis, Mars' burning hour, and Montu is the war god without rival for it. The hexa arm at 16h burns orange — Zeal, the mood of the working afternoon, the ember hours when a campaign is won by refusing to stop. That is Montu's native tempo: not the parade after victory but the march that earns it — the Soldier is this arm's profession, and Montu is the soldier's god, the pharaoh's sword-arm deified.

[[The Lesson]] Mars carries Courage and Wrath, one fire with two uses, and Egypt drew the doctrine straight into this god: Montu is force under the king's command — the khopesh raised FOR Egypt — while berserk rage the Egyptians gave to Sekhmet's rampage, not to him. His remedy stands straight across the dial at 4h, and in this theme it is a neighbor from home: Khonsu, Thebes' own moon god, healer and marker of time, whose Serenity quells Wrath — while Montu sends Courage back along the axis to cure the Moon's Fear. Two Thebans holding opposite ends of the day, the war god and the night-healer keeping each other whole.

variants.hexa_primary: The home arm: 16h, ember orange, Zeal — Montu's campaign hour, the working afternoon when an army either pushes on or breaks; the falcon rides the day's stubborn fire.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette Montu keeps 16h but the ember flares to pure yellow — pigment's orange has no seat in the prism wheel, so the afternoon burns at light's brightest hue. For this god the flare is doctrine: he fused with the sun as Montu-Ra, and the war-arm blazing solar yellow is that fusion drawn in light.
variants.octa_primary: Montu, the falcon war god whose name alone once meant 'fought like a god,' now shares his afternoon arm with copper (#C87533) — the Walk of the Merchant, the Coin his object, a seat that reads at first like defeat for a god of the khopesh. But Thebes never separated the sword from the treasury: war paid for temples, tribute followed conquest, and every campaign Thutmose III or Ramses II fought 'like Montu' filled Egypt's granaries as surely as its armories — the Merchant's Coin was always the war god's other harvest.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel the afternoon arm is Maturity, and Montu takes its amber (#FFB400) as the mid-life register of his own doctrine: not the raw Wrath of a young berserker but Courage seasoned into command, the campaign fought with judgment rather than fury. A warrior-king praised 'like Montu on the battlefield' was never praised as reckless — amber is the color of strength that has already learned restraint.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross Montu takes the 18h dusk arm, red for Autumn, pointing at the autumn equinox — and shares it with Hathor, as Ares shared everything with Aphrodite. Egypt smiles at the pairing: the war god beside the lady of the west at the very hour the sun goes west — war and love on one arm, the year's long evening.
variants.trio: The Trinity moves Montu to 20h, onto Love's red arm beside Hathor — each arm's tip centers its third of the day, and this pair guards the evening from 16h to 24h, with Faith holding 8h to 16h and Hope 0h to 8h. Montu finally wears his own red, and Love reads through him as protection: the garrison on the wall so that Thebes can sleep — courage keeping watch over what is loved.

mercury.base:
[[The Figure]] Thoth is the scribe of the gods — inventor of hieroglyphs, reckoner of years and moons, clerk of the divine court. He is ibis-headed, the curved beak read as the crescent moon he also wears above his brow; his instruments are the scribe's palette and the reed pen, and beside them the ankh, the key of life — for in Egypt to write a name was to keep its owner alive.

[[The Story]] He belongs to Wednesday the way water belongs to the river. The day is Mercury's — Hermes' day, the messenger's day — and the Greeks who met Thoth did not compare the two gods, they merged them: Hermes Trismegistus, the thrice-greatest, is Thoth wearing Greek. Both count, both write, both guide souls across the last border. And Thoth is this dial's own patron besides: when the year ran five days short, he gambled with the Moon and won a sliver of its light to build the five extra days that made the calendar come out true — the reckoner of time literally repaired the clock.

[[On the Dial]] His arm is the bottom of the dial, 0h, midnight, in mourning purple — the mood of Sorrow. Midnight is the mind's hour, and Egypt gave Thoth exactly that shift: in the Hall of Two Truths, deep in the night of the Duat, the heart is weighed against Ma'at's feather, and it is Thoth who stands beside the scales with pen ready, recording the verdict without mercy and without malice. Sorrow rules his hour not as despair but as exactness — the hour of accounting, when the day is weighed honestly because no one is watching except the one whose job is to write it down.

[[The Lesson]] Wednesday's pair is Wisdom and Greed — the same cleverness that understands the world can start counting it instead, and even a hunger for knowing takes greed's shape when pursued without end. The cure comes down the dial's longest road: straight above at noon Amun keeps the crown, the hidden king, Jupiter's crown in Egyptian dress — his Generosity cures Greed, while Thoth's Wisdom travels back up the axis to curb Amun's Excess. The scribe and the king heal each other across the full height of the day, midnight to noon.

variants.hexa_primary: The home arm: the dial's very bottom at 0h, mourning purple (#542E85), the Sorrow of midnight — Thoth beside the scales in the Hall of Two Truths, keeping the night's record on Wednesday's arm.
variants.hexa_secondary: The prism keeps him at 0h but turns the purple to magenta (#BD00BD) — the one hue no rainbow contains, invented by the eye where the spectrum's two ends meet. The inventor of writing wears the invented color: a sign standing for something that is not there, which is what every hieroglyph is.
variants.octa_primary: The ibis-headed scribe takes the late-evening arm in stage-velvet violet (#7A2E8E) — the Walk of the Artist, the Mask its object — an unlikely seat for the god of exact accounting until one remembers Thoth is also Hermes Trismegistus, thrice-great and endlessly disguised across a thousand years of syncretism, one god performing as many masks as cultures needed him to wear. The reed pen that records every verdict in the Hall of Two Truths is, after all, the truest performance in the whole temple.
variants.octa_secondary: On the Ages wheel the same hour deepens to dusk violet (#9C6BD4) — Old Age, the wisdom that comes only after long counting. No god fits it more naturally than the one who reckoned every year of the calendar and gambled with the Moon to win the five days that made the count come out true; Old Age here is not decline but the accumulated exactness of a god who has already written down everything that came before.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross Thoth returns to the bottom arm at 0h, blue for Winter, pointed at the winter solstice — and he holds it alone, the only body that shares its arm with no one. It is the right solitude: the god who added the five days that made the year come out true stands at the year's own midnight, keeping its longest night the way he keeps every record — by himself.
variants.trio: The trio lifts Thoth off midnight to 4h, onto Hope's blue arm (#002FFF) beside the Moon, guarding the morning third from 0h to 8h — and the pairing is an old joke between them, for it was from the Moon that Thoth won the light that lengthened the year. Hope is the theological shape of the scribe's trust in his own ledger: the record is kept at midnight precisely so that morning has something to read.

jupiter.base:
[[The Figure]] Amun is the Hidden One — his name in Egyptian means exactly that, the unseen — a god of air and breath from Thebes who rose to king of the gods, absorbed the sun itself as Amun-Ra, and ruled from Karnak, the largest temple complex the ancient world ever raised. The Greeks did not merely compare him to Zeus; they equated him: Zeus Ammon, whose desert oracle at Siwa Alexander crossed the sands to consult. Thursday is Jupiter's day and Jupiter is Zeus — so the king of Egypt's gods takes the king planet's seat by the ancients' own identification, not ours.

[[On the Dial]] On the hexa paint dial his arm is the crown itself: the top vertex at 12h, yellow, noon — the mood of Joy, at the very tip the star points at true solar noon. 'Jovial' literally means 'of Jupiter,' and Amun's own regalia argues the same seat: gold is noon yellow made solid, and his twin plumes are read upward, exactly where the arm points — straight up, at the day's peak.

[[The Lesson]] Thursday's virtue is Generosity and its vice is Excess, and Amun lived both. Ramesside prayers call him the vizier of the poor, the one who comes at the voice of the humble — generosity from a hidden hand; yet his priesthood at Karnak grew so rich in land and grain that it came to rival the throne itself — the royal table overflowing into an estate. The cure hangs across the dial at midnight: Mercury's Wisdom — on this Egyptian dial Thoth, the scribe who counts — curbs Amun's Excess, while Amun's open hand pours down the same axis to cure the counting god's Greed. The full hand and the counting hand, balancing each other.

variants.hexa_primary: The home arm is the crown of the star: the dial's top at 12h, noon yellow, the mood of Joy — and Amun was made for that seat, the twin plumes of his crown read exactly where the top vertex points, at true solar noon. The king of the gods in gold, on the arm whose color is the day's gold.
variants.hexa_secondary: The light palette keeps Amun at the 12h crown but dresses the arm in green — the middle color of the spectrum, which the prism wheel seats at noon. A fitting robe for the Hidden One: like the god whose name means unseen, green stands at the exact center of the visible band — Joy read as fullness of light rather than gold leaf.
variants.octa_primary: Amun the Hidden One, king of Karnak's priesthood, takes the mid-morning arm in alb ivory (#EDEDE0) — the Walk of the Priest, the Bell his object — the one seat on the wheel that needed no argument at all, since Amun's own temple was the largest the ancient world raised and his clergy all but ran the state's treasury of grain and land. The vizier-of-the-poor who answers 'the voice of the humble' and the priest who rings the temple bell are, in Amun's case, simply the same open hand.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel his morning arm turns spring green (#7CE577) — Childhood, the wheel's freshest hour — and Amun, breath and air made visible, invisible and everywhere, wears it as the youngest register of his own vast patience: the temple day of giving beginning again, small and green, before Karnak's centuries of accumulated gold had piled up around him.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross Amun keeps the top arm at 12h, yellow for Summer, sharing it with the Sun — which in Egyptian dress is simply Amun-Ra spelled out: the hidden king and the visible disc presiding together. The summer solstice is the year at its most generous — the longest light, the season the Nile began to rise and fill the land.
variants.trio: On the Trinity Amun keeps his crown: the 12h arm, yellow — but the yellow is Faith's now, shared with Saturn (Osiris on this dial), and the arm centers the day's third from 8h to 16h with noon at its tip. Faith is the Hidden One's native virtue: Egypt's personal piety prayed to a god no eye could see and trusted that he comes at the voice of the poor — belief in the unseen, practiced daily.

venus.base:
[[The Figure]] Hathor is Egypt's great goddess of love, beauty, music and joy — her name, Hwt-Hr, means "House of Horus": she is the sky itself as a golden house for the falcon sun. Mistress of dance and of the festival of drunkenness at Dendera, mother and lover in one figure, she is also the Lady of the West, who stands at the sunset horizon to receive the dying sun — and the dead — into the evening land. The Greeks who met her knew exactly whom they were looking at and called her Aphrodite without hesitation. Egypt named her besides the Mistress of Turquoise, patroness of the Sinai mines where the sky's own blue-green stone was dug.

[[On the Dial]] She belongs to Friday because Friday belongs to the evening star. Venus opens over the western horizon just after sunset — precisely the sky Hathor rules as Lady of the West — so goddess and planet literally share a station: the most beautiful light in the heavens standing over the gate of the dead. On the hexa paint dial her arm is 20h, deep red, the mood of Passion — the hour when work ends and wanting begins, when the sunset bleeds and the music starts at Dendera.

[[The Lesson]] Love is her virtue and Jealousy her vice — love's shadow, not its opposite. Egypt told that shadow plainly: as the Eye of Ra she withdrew from the land in bitterness and had to be coaxed home with music and dance, and once, unleashed, only beer dyed red as blood could still her — love turned resentful until joy calls it back. The cure stands straight across the dial at 8h, on the green morning arm this theme gives to Osiris: Patience heals Jealousy, and Hathor's Love flows back across the axis to dissolve Envy. It is the dial's most Egyptian axis — the Lady of the West delivers the dead to the lord of rebirth, and love and patience have passed between those two since the first sunset.

variants.hexa_primary: The home arm: 20h, blood red, Passion — the Lady of the West on the arm of the evening she rules, the sistrum shaking as the sun goes down into her country.
variants.hexa_secondary: The light palette keeps Hathor at 20h and turns her red to the prism's full voltage — pure red, light's own primary. Passion undiluted: the goddess of the drunkenness festival poured the strongest red that light itself can mix.
variants.octa_primary: Hathor, the Lady of the West who receives the dying sun into evening, now shares the sunset arm with iron-blood crimson (#A02020) — the Walk of the Soldier, the Sword its object, an estate her gentle sistrum never asked for. Yet Egypt knew her fiercer face too: unleashed as the Eye of Ra she rampaged until only blood-red beer could still her, and a goddess capable of that fury wears a Soldier's crimson more honestly than her turquoise first suggests.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel her sunset arm turns ember (#FF6A3C) — the Elder, the harvest of a life — and no goddess sits it more fittingly: Hathor stands at the horizon precisely to gather in the dying sun and the dying alike, the evening's harvest of a whole day's light collected into her own hands before the dark takes it.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross Hathor holds the 18h arm, red for Autumn, sharing it with Montu — love and war on one arm, as Egypt itself told it: the lady of joy and the Eye of Ra are one goddess in two moods, and Thebes worshipped her beside its falcon of battle. The autumn equinox is the year's dusk — the harvest of what was loved, carried west.
variants.trio: Hathor does not move at all: the Trinity's red Love arm is her own 20h, and Love is already her whole estate — the one virtue standing in both the seven pairs and the theological three. Montu joins her there, and together they guard the evening from 16h to 24h: music on one side of the door and a raised arm on the other, passion and courage keeping the dark third of the day.

saturn.base:
[[The Figure]] Before he was lord of the dead, Osiris was the king who taught Egypt to grow grain — the myth remembers him as the first civilizer, murdered and cut into pieces by his brother Set, who envied the throne. Isis gathered him, love reassembling what envy had scattered, and the risen god took the throne of the underworld instead: judge of hearts, first of the westerners, the one every Egyptian hoped to become at death — the funerary texts promote each soul into 'an Osiris'. His death and return were read into everything that cycles: the Nile flood, the buried seed, the grain that stands again.

[[On the Dial]] He rules Saturday because Osiris is Saturn's patience made a god. Cronus carries the harvest sickle; Osiris owned the harvest first, and the flail on his chest is a threshing tool as much as a scepter. Saturn takes nearly thirty years to close one circle, and no figure in any pantheon out-waits Osiris — he waits out death itself and comes back green. On the day of rest, whose planet in Hebrew is Shabtai after the Sabbath, Egypt's god rests in the earth the way seed does: temporarily.

[[The Lesson]] The arm gives him green at 8h, the morning, the mood of Renewal — and Egypt agreed millennia in advance, painting Osiris's skin green as new growth, exactly the field his arm glows with. Patience is the arm's virtue: the seed's whole art is waiting in the dark. Envy is its vice, and Osiris knows it from the receiving end — Set's envy is the engine of the entire myth. The cure stands across the dial on the red evening arm: Venus' Love — Hathor's, in this theme — dissolves Envy, just as Isis's love regathered the dismembered king; and Saturn's Patience travels back to heal Venus' Jealousy — the waiting art and the loving art mending each other.

variants.hexa_primary: The home arm: 8h, morning green (#007E00), Renewal — Saturday, the week's rest and restart. Paint green is Osiris's own pigment: tomb painters gave him skin this color to mean rebirth, and the arm simply widens that malachite to fill a whole sixth of the dial.
variants.hexa_secondary: The light palette keeps him at 8h but turns the green to cyan (#00DDDD) — morning read as water-light rather than field. For Osiris that is the Nile's color: the flood that buried the fields each year and left them fertile was called his coming.
variants.octa_primary: Osiris, the king who first taught Egypt to grow grain, takes the dawn arm in field green (#3E8914) — the Walk of the Farmer, the Plough its object — the one seat on this whole wheel that asks no translation whatsoever. The crook and flail crossed on his mummiform chest were farming tools before they were royal regalia, and a god whose green skin already meant new growth simply steps into the estate he founded.
variants.octa_secondary: On the Ages wheel the dawn arm is Birth, and Osiris wears its predawn mist (#8FA8C8) — the hour Ra's barque leaves the underworld, and the exact threshold Osiris himself crosses every time a soul is 'made an Osiris' at death and promised rebirth. No god on the dial has out-waited death more thoroughly; Birth here is simply his oldest and most literal specialty, dressed in the color of the hour just before the light returns.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross Osiris holds the 6h arm, green for Spring, pointed at the vernal equinox and shared with the Moon — Khonsu in this theme. Sowing season is his festival in the most literal sense: Egyptians planted 'Osiris beds', seed grain in god-shaped molds, and watched the deity himself sprout.
variants.trio: The Trinity promotes him from the morning to the crown: the 12h Faith arm, yellow (#F8E600), shared with Jupiter — Amun here — guarding the day's height from 8h to 16h. Faith reads through Osiris as the oldest resurrection promise there is: every tomb in Egypt was built on trust that what goes into the earth comes back — the harvest creed spoken toward the sky.

sun.base:
[[The Figure]] Dažbog is the giving sun — his very name binds dati, to give, to bog, god: the god who gives. He is the son of Svarog the sky-smith, and he rides the daylight across the heavens in a chariot, dealing out warmth and grain and fortune to whoever stands beneath him. The Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the Slavs themselves Dažbog's grandchildren, vnutsi Dazhbozhi — a whole people descended from the sun, warmed by an ancestor who asks nothing and pours out everything.

[[On the Dial]] His day is Sunday — nedelja in the Slavic tongue, the 'no-work' day, the day the week rests in the light before it begins again. So Dažbog does not take an arm at all: he holds the CENTER of the dial, white-gold, the still hub from which the six colored arms radiate. He is the source the whole spectrum decomposes from — white light that only looks empty because it already contains every color the other gods will wear.

[[The Lesson]] Dažbog gives all his light away and keeps none for himself — that endless open-handed giving is the deepest Humility, and its shadow is the Pride that would hoard the blaze and call the warmth its own, the one axis whose cure sits in the center it came from. Yet the center is DOUBLE, two virtues, two vices, two moods in one seat, and the GIVING god's very name splits the same way: he is king and servant at once, the ancestor-lord of the Slavs who nevertheless hands out the day like bread, every morning, to everyone. That even-handed giving is his Justice; giving reduced to bare obligation would be his Servility. His Glory is the high summer he pours from the horn — and his Awe the winter dimming, when the grandfather of the people walks his road old and gray, trusting the spring to crown him again.

variants.hexa_primary: In the paint palette the center is the one color no brush can reach: pigments mix by subtraction, and no blending of pigments ever yields white. So Dažbog's white-gold hub is the unmixable center — the source every colored arm is a piece of, yet none of them, mixed, can climb back up to. He can give the colors out; they can never give him back.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette the logic reverses: the six colored beams of the arms, summed at the hub, add up to exactly white. Here Dažbog's white-gold center is not a paint that cannot be mixed but a radiance that is the sum of all six — the giving sun proven by arithmetic, every arm's color returning to make the light whole again.
variants.octa_primary: Dažbog, the giving sun whose name means simply 'the god who gives,' steps from the dial's center onto the noon arm in royal gold (#F0C420) — the Walk of the King, the Crown his object — a seat this ancestor-lord already half-occupies, since The Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the Slavs his own grandchildren, warmed and ruled by one radiant ancestor. The horn of plenty he carries was always a king's largesse before it was a Compass arm's harvest.
variants.octa_secondary: On the Ages wheel the noon arm is Youth, and Dažbog wears its sun-yellow (#FFE800) as the blazing register of his own myth: the light he pours out endlessly, high summer poured from the horn, strength before any descent. A god who rides the daylight chariot at full strength each day was already living at the zenith the Ages wheel now simply names.
variants.cross: The seasons cross keeps a true crossing — four arms meeting at one point — and Dažbog keeps that meeting-place, the hub where the year's four quarters intersect. The giving sun holds the still center around which spring, summer, autumn and winter wheel, the fixed white-gold heart of the turning year.
variants.trio: In the trio — Faith, Hope, Love — the sun keeps the center, and from it the yellow Faith arm rises straight up the 12h vertical (Faith at top, Hope at 4h, Love at 20h). Dažbog is the white-gold source, and Faith is the first thing that climbs out of him toward noon: the giving light made into the upward-pointing virtue.

faces.ruler:
Young Dažbog is the Ruler face — the giving sun, his very name binding dati, to give, to bog, god, son of Svarog the sky-smith, ancestor of a people the old chronicles call his own grandchildren.

His virtue is Justice, the day handed out like bread to everyone beneath him without exception, king and peasant warmed by the same beam — but that even-handedness is stalked by Pride, the temptation to believe the horn empties because he chooses to be generous rather than because giving is simply what a sun does. His mood is Glory, high summer poured freely from the horn, the corona at its widest and the wheat at its ripest.
faces.servant:
Old Dažbog is the Servant face — not a second god but the same giving sun grown gray, the ancestor of the Slavs walking his road in winter instead of riding it in high summer.

His virtue is Humility, the giving god admitting the horn runs low and trusting the spring to refill it rather than pretending the bounty is endless — and Servility is what the winter reduces him to if that trust curdles into mere plodding, the ancestor walking only because the road demands it. His mood is Awe, the winter dimming the whole people wait out — and Glory is the same grandfather crowned again every spring, young once more.

moon.base:
[[The Figure]] Hors is the light of the night — the cold luminary that rules the sky when the sun is gone. His name may carry the old Iranian root for glow or sun-disc, and he moves as a wheel of pale fire across the dark. The Tale of Igor's Campaign remembers him in one unforgettable line: prince Vseslav the sorcerer, running as a wolf through the night, 'crossed the path of great Hors' before the cockcrow — a werewolf racing the moon's own track and cutting across it in the last dark before dawn.

[[On the Dial]] His day is Monday — ponedeljak, the day 'after nedelja,' the first step out of the day of rest and still half in the dark. Hors takes the 4h arm, low on the left of the dial, in deep blue — the hour just before dawn, when the night's light is thinnest and the world is most still. His mood is Calm: the held breath of the last dark hour before the sun returns.

[[The Lesson]] His axis is Serenity against Fear. The dark is where fear breeds — every shape a threat, every sound a wolf — and Hors answers it with the Serenity of a steady night-light that does not flinch. His cure lies across the dial in the mars arm: the Courage of Svetovid is what dissolves the Fear that the moonlit dark invents. Calm holds the night; courage ends it.

variants.hexa_primary: In the paint palette Hors holds the 4h arm in a deep blue (#002FFF) — the pigment of the pre-dawn hour, night thinned but not yet broken. It is the mixing-blue of the darkest part of the wheel, the color the world wears in the last cold hour before Dažbog climbs back over the rim.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette the same 4h arm burns as pure primary blue (#0040FF) — one of the three beams the white hub decomposes into. Hors is no longer a mixed pigment but a fundamental ray: the blue that light itself is built from, the night's own frequency standing clean in the prism wheel.
variants.octa_primary: Hors, the cold luminary who crosses the night as a wheel of pale fire, settles onto the deep-night arm in lamplit ink blue (#1F5FA8) — the Walk of the Scholar, the Book his object. The Tale of Igor's Campaign already reads him as a measured track that even a sorcerer-prince must 'cross,' a fixed and countable path across the dark — the Scholar's arm simply gives that path its proper shelf and pen.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel his arm turns moonlight silver (#C8D7F0) — the Unborn, ancestors and not-yet-born together — a fitting hue for a wheel of pale fire whose phases wax from nothing and wane back to nothing every month, the same nightly disappearance and return that Hors performs while Vseslav the werewolf races across his track before the cockcrow.
variants.cross: The seasons cross moves Hors to the 6h arm, colored spring green and aimed straight at the vernal equinox — and here he shares the arm with Morana, the saturn body. The night-light and the winter-death stand on the same spring arm: for the dawn to come and the year to turn, the long dark and the frost must both give way at once.
variants.trio: In the trio Hors keeps the 4h arm, but it is now the Hope arm, colored Hope blue (#002FFF) — and he shares it with Veles, the mercury body. The last dark hour becomes the hour of Hope: the moon-light that outlasts the night is the promise that the sun will rise, blue leaning toward the coming gold.

mars.base:
[[The Figure]] Svetovid was the great war-god of the western Slavs, worshipped at the temple of Arkona on the island of Rügen until the Danes threw it down in 1168. His idol had FOUR faces, one gazing to each of the four directions, so that nothing on any horizon escaped him. His priests refilled a horn of mead before the idol every year and read it as an omen: a full horn promised a fat harvest, a low one warned of famine. And in the temple he kept a sacred WHITE HORSE that only the priest could ride — before any campaign they led it over crossed spears, and the foot it stepped with first told the army whether the god blessed the war.

[[On the Dial]] His day is Tuesday — utorak, simply 'the second,' the second day of labor. Svetovid takes the 16h arm on the lower right of the dial, burning ember orange, and his mood is Zeal — the hard driving heat of the working afternoon, the hour when the day's fight is fully joined and the arms swing without pause.

[[The Lesson]] His axis is Courage against Wrath. The war-god is Courage itself — the nerve to lead the white horse over the spears and march — but his shadow is Wrath, the battle-heat that stops being brave and starts being blind. His cure waits across the dial in the moon arm: the Serenity of Hors is what quells the Wrath, the cool night-calm laid over the ember of the fight.

variants.hexa_primary: In the paint palette Svetovid holds the 16h arm in ember orange — a mixed pigment, red warmed with yellow, the exact color of iron pulled glowing from the forge. It is the afternoon at its hottest, the war-heat given a hue you can only reach by blending, a fighting color mixed from blood and fire.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette orange has no seat — the prism wheel knows no orange among its beams — so Svetovid's arm resolves to pure yellow instead. The war-god, denied his ember, stands in the raw yellow of open daylight: the Zeal is the same, but the color is stripped back to a ray the prism actually contains.
variants.octa_primary: Svetovid, the four-faced war-god of Arkona, shares his working-afternoon arm with copper (#C87533) — the Walk of the Merchant, the Coin its object — a strange seat for a god who led the sacred white horse to war, until his own temple's practice is remembered: the mead-horn his priests read each year was itself an economic omen, a full horn promising harvest, a low one warning of scarcity. The war-god who blessed campaigns also kept, quite literally, the treasury's forecast in his own hand.
variants.octa_secondary: On the Ages wheel his arm turns amber (#FFB400) — Maturity, strength seasoned rather than raw — and Svetovid wears it as the four-faced god who watches every horizon at once, a readiness that has outgrown any single reckless charge. The white horse only stepped over the crossed spears once the priests had judged the year mature enough to risk it.
variants.cross: The seasons cross moves Svetovid to the 18h dusk arm, colored red and aimed at the autumn equinox — and he shares it with Mokoš, the venus body. The war-god and the earth-mother stand together on the arm of harvest's end: autumn is the season armies march and the season the fields are cut, dusk-red for both the blade and the sickle.
variants.trio: In the trio Svetovid moves to the 20h Love arm, colored red, standing beside Mokoš and guarding the evening third of the dial from 16h to 24h. The war-god posted on the Love arm is the guardian's paradox — the sword that stands watch so the evening can be loved in peace, Courage set to keep the hours it does not spend fighting.

mercury.base:
[[The Figure]] Veles — Volos in the old treaties — is the horned god of everything that lives low and moves in the dark: cattle and wealth, trade and cunning, music and magic, and the underworld of the dead. He is the 'cattle-god,' skotiy bog, and when the Rus' princes swore peace with Byzantium they swore it 'by Perun and by Volos' — the thunderer for their weapons, the cattle-god for their goods. He is the serpent coiled at the roots of the world-tree while Perun holds its crown, and he is the patron of poets: the Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the great bard Boyan 'Veles's grandson.'

[[On the Dial]] His day is Wednesday — sreda, 'the middle,' the hinge of the week. Veles takes the very BOTTOM of the dial, the 0h/24h arm at midnight, in mourning purple — the day's grave, the deepest dark, the mystery under everything. His mood is Sorrow. And his position is the myth itself: Veles at the bottom and Perun at the crown of the star is the Perun–Veles axis made literal — the serpent at the roots, the thunderer at the top, the two poles of the vertical the whole dial hangs from.

[[The Lesson]] His axis is Wisdom against Greed. The underworld-god is Wisdom — the deep, buried knowing of the dead, the cunning of trade, the poet's craft — but the same appetite that gathers cattle and coin curdles into Greed, the hoard kept for its own sake. His cure is across the dial: the Generosity of the jupiter arm, the open hand of the thunder-god's rain, is what dissolves the serpent's Greed. Wisdom knows what to keep; generosity knows what to give away.

variants.hexa_primary: In the paint palette Veles holds the 0h arm in mourning purple (#542E85) — a mixed, bruised color, red and blue ground together into the hue of grief and midnight. It is the pigment of the day's grave, the deepest, most blended dark on the wheel, the color of the underworld the cattle-god keeps.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette his purple resolves to magenta (#BD00BD) — the strange color the prism itself cannot make, that only appears where the spectrum's two ends are bent around to touch. Fitting for the god of the boundary between living and dead: Veles wears the one hue that lives outside the rainbow, at the bottom where the ends meet.
variants.octa_primary: Veles, the horned cattle-god and patron of poets — Boyan the bard was called 'Veles's grandson' — takes the late-evening arm in stage-velvet violet (#7A2E8E), the Walk of the Artist and its Mask, a seat his own lyre had already half-earned. The serpent coiled at the world-tree's root and the singer coiled around a verse are, in Veles, one and the same cunning performance.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel the arm deepens to dusk violet (#9C6BD4) — Old Age — and Veles, god of the underworld and of the dead's own deep knowing, wears it as the accumulated wisdom of the buried: not decline but the cunning of trade and song that only comes from having watched every generation of cattle, coin, and poet pass beneath his roots.
variants.cross: The seasons cross keeps Veles on the 0h arm, aimed at the winter solstice and colored winter blue — and alone. Every other body shares its seasonal arm; the cattle-god shares none. The god of the longest night holds the year's longest night by himself, the serpent at the bottom of the year as well as of the dial, unpartnered in the deepest dark.
variants.trio: In the trio Veles climbs to the 4h Hope arm, colored Hope blue (#002FFF), and shares it with Hors, the moon body. The underworld-god rises out of the grave to stand on the arm of Hope beside the night-light — the buried Wisdom leaning toward dawn, the serpent lifting its head at the promise of morning.

jupiter.base:
[[The Figure]] Perun is the thunder-god, the axe-bearer, the chief of the old Slavic sky. His tree is the oak, his weapon the axe and the hurled thunderstone, and his sign is the six-petalled thunder-mark — the gromovnik rosette that Slavs carved into their roof-beams to turn the lightning away, a six-armed star the clock's own hexagram pointer quietly echoes. His great myth is the storm itself: the serpent Veles steals the cattle and dams up the waters, and Perun hunts him across the sky and strikes him with the bolt — and the RAIN that bursts loose is the sky's generosity, the withheld water finally given back to the earth.

[[On the Dial]] His day is Thursday — četvrtak, 'the fourth' — and on the dial he takes the TOP, the 12h arm, the crown of the star, in noon yellow. His mood is Joy: the high, ringing gladness of the sky at its brightest, the thunder-god at the zenith. That the six-armed hexagram crowns him at the top is no accident — the pointer is his own thunder-mark, and he sits at the head of it.

[[The Lesson]] His axis is Generosity against Excess. The rain he releases is pure Generosity — the sky opening its hand and pouring the hoarded water down onto the fields — but the same storm can drown what it means to feed, and that is Excess, the flood that gives too hard. His cure is across the dial in the mercury arm: the Wisdom of Veles, the serpent he strikes, is exactly what curbs the Excess. The old enemies balance each other — the thunderer's giving needs the serpent's knowing-when-to-stop.

variants.hexa_primary: In the paint palette Perun crowns the 12h arm in noon yellow — the pure high pigment of midday, the brightest color the wheel puts at the top. The thunder-mark's crown-petal glows the yellow of the sky at noon, Joy given the boldest hue on the dial, straight up where the light is highest.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette the top arm resolves to green — because green sits at the exact middle of the visible spectrum, and the middle of the spectrum belongs at the middle of the crown. Perun's noon becomes green here: the thunder-god wearing the balance-point of all light, the center wavelength raised to the zenith.
variants.octa_primary: Perun, the thunder-god whose six-petalled gromovnik already echoes the clock's own hexagram, takes the mid-morning arm in alb ivory (#EDEDE0) — the Walk of the Priest, the Bell his object — and the fit runs deeper than costume: the thunder-mark was carved into roof-beams as a ward, a household rite as devout as any bell rung in a nave. The axe that strikes Veles free from his dam is, seen from the Priest's arm, simply the storm performing its own liturgy.
variants.octa_secondary: On the Ages wheel his arm turns spring green (#7CE577) — Childhood — and Perun wears it as the freshest register of the rain he releases: the fields fed newly each spring, the storm's Generosity read as growth just beginning rather than the flood of Excess it can also become.
variants.cross: The seasons cross keeps Perun at the 12h arm, colored yellow and aimed at the summer solstice — and he shares it with Dažbog, the sun body. The thunder-god and the giving sun stand together at the top of the year: high summer is the season of both the ripening light and the ripening storm, the sun and the rain crowning the dial as one.
variants.trio: In the trio Perun keeps the crown at 12h, now the Faith arm in Faith yellow, shared with Morana, the saturn body — and he guards the day third of the dial from 8h to 16h. The thunder-god at the top of the vertical holds the arm of Faith over the bright working hours, the storm-crown turned into the keystone of the day.

venus.base:
[[The Figure]] Mokoš is the great goddess — the only goddess Prince Vladimir set among the idols of his Kyiv pantheon, standing alone among the gods. She is the spinner: the flax and the wool, the distaff and the thread, and by extension the thread of fate itself, measured out and cut. And she is Moist Mother Earth, Mati Syra Zemlya, the damp fertile ground her very name seems to hold — mok-, the wet. When Christianity came she did not die but changed her name to St Paraskeva-Pyatnitsa, 'Friday,' venerated on the day that was already hers, where it stayed forbidden to spin.

[[On the Dial]] Her day is Friday — petak in the Slavic count, 'the fifth,' but her true name for it is Pyatnitsa, the day of St Paraskeva, when no woman spun for fear of her. On the dial she takes the 20h arm, deep in the evening, in blood red, and her mood is Passion — the warm red heat of the evening hours, the fire of love and of the hearth after the day's work is done.

[[The Lesson]] Her axis is Love against Jealousy. Mokoš is Love itself — the fertile, binding, life-spinning love of the earth-mother — but its shadow is Jealousy, the love that clenches into possession and fear of loss. Her cure is across the dial in the saturn arm: the Patience of Morana, the long slow patience of the ground that waits through winter, is what heals the Jealousy. Love that can wait does not need to grasp.

variants.hexa_primary: In the paint palette Mokoš holds the 20h arm in blood red — the deep mixed crimson of the evening, of the hearth-fire and the ripe fruit and the blood of birth. It is the warmest pigment on the lower dial, the color of Passion given body, the evening turned the red of love.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette her arm resolves to pure red — one of the three primary beams the white hub breaks into. Mokoš's evening becomes a fundamental ray: not the mixed crimson of the pigment but the clean elemental red that light itself is built from, Passion stripped to its root frequency.
variants.octa_primary: Mokoš, the spinner of fate and Moist Mother Earth — the only goddess Vladimir set among his idols — shares her evening arm with iron-blood crimson (#A02020), the Walk of the Soldier, the Sword its object. It reads against her gentle distaff until the ground itself is remembered as the guarded thing: earth is what every army has ever marched to keep, and the goddess who is the soil holds the Sword the way a mother holds the door.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel her arm turns ember (#FF6A3C) — the Elder, the harvest of a life — and Mokoš wears it plainly: she is Moist Mother Earth, and no figure on the dial is more literally the harvest itself, the sheaves at her side already the gathered work of a whole season's growing.
variants.cross: The seasons cross sets Mokoš on the 18h dusk arm, colored red and aimed at the autumn equinox — shared with Svetovid, the mars body. The earth-mother and the war-god stand together on the harvest arm: autumn is when the wheat she spins beside is cut and when the armies march, the sickle and the sword sharing one red dusk.
variants.trio: In the trio Mokoš keeps the 20h arm — and here the red Love arm is truly hers, the virtue that is her whole nature made into a direction. She shares it with Svetovid, the mars body: the earth-mother's Love and the war-god's guard on the same evening arm, the thing worth loving and the sword that keeps it.

saturn.base:
[[The Figure]] Morana is the goddess of winter and of death — Marzanna, Mara, Morena, her name rooted in the old word for death itself. She is the cold that kills the year, and every spring the Slavs kill her back: they build her as a straw effigy, dress her, carry her out of the village in procession, and drown or burn her at the vernal equinox to end the winter and let the spring in. The custom is still alive across the Slavic lands. She is death not as an end but as a hinge — the dying the world has to pass through before it can be born again.

[[On the Dial]] Her day is Saturday — subota, the old Sabbath, the week's edge and its rest. Yet on the dial she takes the 8h arm in morning green, and her mood is Renewal — which for the death-goddess is the whole point. She sits at the hour of the week's rest and restart, the green of new morning, because the one who ends the year is also the one who clears the ground for it to begin again.

[[The Lesson]] Her axis is Patience against Envy. Morana is Patience — the deep, frozen, waiting patience of winter and of the buried dead, the long stillness that outlasts everything — and her shadow is Envy, the cold resentment of the living and the warm. Her cure is across the dial in the venus arm: the Love of Mokoš, the warm earth-mother, is what dissolves the Envy. Winter's patience and spring's love are the same hinge seen from its two sides.

variants.hexa_primary: In the paint palette Morana holds the 8h arm in morning green (#007E00) — a mixed pigment, blue cooled into yellow, the green of new grass under the last frost. It is the strangest color on her: the death-goddess given the hue of first growth, Renewal painted in the green of the morning her winter finally releases.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette her arm resolves to cyan (#00DDDD) — the cold bright blue-green of ice and thaw-water. Morana's morning turns to cyan here, the exact color of meltwater and winter light, the death-goddess wearing the hue of the very thaw that drowns her effigy.
variants.octa_primary: Morana, the winter goddess whose straw effigy is drowned each spring to end the cold, takes the dawn arm in field green (#3E8914) — the Walk of the Farmer, the Plough its object — the one seat that needs no translation. She is death as a hinge, not an end, and the Slavs who burn her at the equinox are performing exactly what a farmer performs each fallow season: clearing the old growth so the plough can turn new ground.
variants.octa_secondary: On the Ages wheel her arm turns predawn mist (#8FA8C8) — Birth — and no goddess on the dial earns the paradox more honestly: Morana is winter and death made flesh, yet her whole ritual exists to be ended, drowned each spring so the year can be born again. Birth is simply her death read forward instead of back.
variants.cross: The seasons cross moves Morana to the 6h arm, colored spring green and aimed straight at the vernal equinox — shared with Hors, the moon body. For her this is the most literal arm on the dial: the vernal equinox is the exact day her straw effigy is drowned. The death-goddess pointed at the very moment of her own drowning, standing on the hinge where winter dies into spring.
variants.trio: In the trio Morana is promoted all the way to the 12h crown, the Faith arm in Faith yellow (#F8E600), shared with Perun, the jupiter body. The death-goddess raised to the top of the star holds the arm of Faith beside the thunder-god — because the deepest Faith is the one that trusts the dying: that winter drowned is spring promised, the effigy in the river the year reborn.

sun.base:
[[The Figure]] Gold is the sun brought to earth: the one metal that never rusts, never tarnishes, never dulls — incorruptible, and therefore, to the alchemists, perfect. It is the goal of the whole Great Work, the magnum opus that climbs from black nigredo through white albedo and yellow citrinitas to red rubedo, and the sign for gold and the sign for the Sun are the same circle with a central point. Soft enough to beat into leaf a few atoms thick, dense enough to sink in any river, gold was money, crown, and reliquary at once — "as above, so below," the sun's own light made solid.

[[On the Dial]] Sunday is the Sun's day in plain sight — Sunday, Sonntag, dies Solis — so gold takes the day and the very center of the dial. On the hexagram, the cross, and the trio it sits at the hub, the white-gold source from which all six colors of the star decompose, the way a prism unfolds one white beam into a spectrum. Only on the octa does it leave home, stepping up to the topmost 12h arm to blaze as noon itself.

[[The Lesson]] Gold sits at the heart of everything yet asks for nothing — Pride is the false gold, all glare and no warmth, while Humility is the true, the white light that gives itself to every color and keeps none, answering Pride not by dimming but by shining evenly on all. Yet the center is DOUBLE, two virtues, two vices, two moods in one seat, a doubleness assayers know by trade: gold is the standard every metal is measured against, which is Justice itself, and at the same time the most obedient servant in the shop — coined, alloyed, beaten to leaf a breath thick. Servility is gold spent as mere money; Pride is gold worshiped as more than metal. Its Glory is the incorruptible shine no age can tarnish — and its Awe the same metal buried nameless in the ore, waiting for the Work to call it out.

variants.hexa_primary: On the hexagram in pigment, gold holds the unmixable center. No two paints ever blend into white — white is where paint runs out — so the goldsmith does not mix it at all: he lays it on as leaf, beaten to gossamer and pressed whole onto the surface. The six colored arms radiate from a hub that can only be gilded, never ground. It is Humility as a technique — the one color you receive rather than make.
variants.hexa_secondary: On the hexagram in prism light, the trick reverses. Here white is not the absence of color but the sum of all of it: the six colored beams run inward and meet at the hub, and where they overlap they add to pure white-gold light. The Sun is what the whole star adds up to. Gold, in light, is Humility rewarded — every arm gives its hue, and their gift, combined, is the source shining back.
variants.octa_primary: Gold, the metal that never tarnishes, takes the noon arm and needs no new coat of paint at all — the wheel's royal gold (#F0C420) for the Walk of the King and his Crown IS gold's own color, the Great Work's own goal made literal. No metal on the dial sits its Walk more exactly: the incorruptible metal was already money, crown, and reliquary before any wheel assigned it an estate.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel the noon arm is Youth, and gold wears sun-yellow (#FFE800) as the blazing target of the whole magnum opus — the rubedo's promised endpoint, matter perfected into the one substance time cannot age. Youth suits it exactly: gold is the metal alchemy calls incorruptible, unaging by definition.
variants.cross: The cross is the seasons palette, four arms for the two solstices and two equinoxes — and gold keeps the crossing at their heart, the still point where all four seasons meet. The year turns around it: summer up, winter down, the equinoxes left and right, and the Sun at the axis that never moves. It is Humility as geometry — the center that lets everything else revolve, and takes no season for its own.
variants.trio: The trio is Faith, Hope and Love — three arms from a single root — and gold keeps the center where that root is anchored. From it the yellow Faith arm rises straight up the 12h line, with Hope at 4h and Love at 20h fanning below. The Sun is the source all three virtues draw from; Faith is simply gold pointing at noon. Humility holds the hub so that Faith, Hope and Love can each reach outward.

faces.ruler:
Gold is the Ruler face — the sun brought to earth, the one metal that never rusts, tarnishes or dulls, the incorruptible goal the whole Great Work climbs toward from black nigredo to red rubedo.

Its virtue is Justice, the standard every other metal is measured against, scales in hand, showing no favor to lead or to silver — but that same standing is stalked by Pride, gold worshiped as more than metal, glare mistaken for warmth. Its mood is Glory, the incorruptible shine no age can tarnish.
faces.servant:
Raw Ore is the Servant face — not a different metal but the same gold before the Work has called it out, still buried, still nameless, waiting in the rock rather than resting on a shelf.

Its virtue is Humility, gold content simply to be gold without yet being praised for it, asking nothing while it waits in the dark — and Servility is what the ore becomes if it is spent as mere rock, never assayed, never called forward into the Work at all. Its mood is Awe, the corona buried and unseen — and Glory is exactly what the Work promises: the same vein, one day refined, shining evenly on everyone who looks at it.

moon.base:
[[The Figure]] Silver is the moon's metal, the white counterpart to gold's yellow, and the alchemists gave it the albedo — the whitening, the second stage of the Work where the blackened prima materia is washed pure. Its sign is a crescent. Silver is the brightest reflector known, which is why every good mirror and every telescope's coating is silver; it throws back the light it is given rather than making its own, exactly as the Moon returns the Sun's. And silver tarnishes — it blackens in the air — so the metal itself keeps the moon's own habit of waxing bright and waning dark.

[[On the Dial]] Monday is the Moon's day and says so — Monday, Montag, lundi, lunes — so silver holds it. On the hexagram the Moon takes the 4h arm, deep blue, the last cold hour before dawn when the sky is darkest and the mood is Calm. The blue is the moon's night: not the fear of the dark but the quiet inside it. Of all the arms this is the one that waits — the hour that knows morning is coming and does not hurry it.

[[The Lesson]] Silver's virtue is Serenity and its vice is Fear, the two faces of the dark. The same night that steadies one mind terrifies another; the mirror shows you whatever you bring to it. Fear is cured from across the dial by Courage on the Mars arm — the iron nerve that meets the ember afternoon — while Serenity is Fear already answered, the still blue that has made its peace with the hour before dawn. Silver keeps Calm by reflecting, never by resisting.

variants.hexa_primary: On the hexagram in pigment, silver keeps the 4h arm in deep blue (#002FFF) — the darkest ground of the wheel, the hour before dawn mixed as a heavy night-blue. Paint reaches its coldest here; there is no bluer blue anywhere on the wheel. It is Serenity ground into color: the calm of the last dark hour, laid thick where the star runs closest to midnight.
variants.hexa_secondary: On the hexagram in prism light, the 4h arm burns as pure primary blue (#0040FF) — one of the three lights the whole spectrum is built from. In pigment blue is a mood; in light it is a foundation. The Moon becomes elemental here, a clean cold beam that the other hues need before they can make anything. Serenity, in light, is not dimness but a primary — the calm the rest of the star is composed from.
variants.octa_primary: Silver, the moon's own metal and the alchemists' albedo, takes the deep-night arm in lamplit ink blue (#1F5FA8) — the Walk of the Scholar, the Book his object — a fitting turn for the metal of every mirror and telescope lens, the reflective surface through which knowledge is literally gathered. What silver returns of borrowed light, the Scholar returns as recorded understanding.
variants.octa_secondary: On the Ages wheel the same arm turns moonlight silver (#C8D7F0) — the Unborn — and here the metal and the hue nearly merge into one: silver was already the whitening stage of the Work, the washed-pure state the black prima materia passes through before it can become anything else, matter suspended exactly between what it was and what it is not yet.
variants.cross: The cross is the seasons, and it moves the Moon to the 6h arm — the spring equinox, colored spring green — and gives her a partner: she shares the arm with Lead, the Saturn metal. Silver and lead at the vernal balance, the brightest metal beside the dullest, the moon of the albedo standing where the year turns from dark to light. Serenity here is the calm of equinox, day and night in perfect equal measure.
variants.trio: On the trio the Moon holds her 4h arm, but it is now the Hope arm, colored Hope blue (#002FFF) — and she shares it with Quicksilver, the Mercury metal. Silver and quicksilver together on the arm of Hope: the two lunar-bright metals, one solid and one liquid, pointing the same blue at the coming dawn. Serenity and Hope are the same gesture here — the calm that waits is also the calm that expects.

mars.base:
[[The Figure]] Iron is the soldier's metal and the planet Mars made solid — the blade, the ploughshare, the nail, and the armor.
