The Choleric holds the summer arm because his humor and the season share both qualities: yellow bile is hot and dry, and so is the year at its height. Hippocrates' oldest account of man survives because it is a temperament theory before it is a medical one, and this wheel keeps it for that reason — four dispositions, each with a bright face and a dark one. His bright face is drive and decisiveness, the Commander who supplies the motion everyone else waits for; his dark face is Wrath and tyranny, the fire that turns on the house it was lit to warm. The seat is the year's longest yellow, the arm this dial already reads as Joy, and his kinship with the Boss syndrome is the Trinity's own diagnosis restated in humors. "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty" (Proverbs 16:32).

His age is The Prime — the noon of a life, powers at their full, the summer of a man. Across the humor square his total opposite is the Phlegmatic (summer against winter, fire against water — the one pair opposed in BOTH qualities), and the winter Calm is the cure his fire most needs.

The Melancholic holds the autumn arm because black bile is cold and dry, exactly as the season is. He is the Thinker: depth bought with heaviness, the humor the classical tradition assigned to scholars and artists because it is the only one that attends to what has already passed. His bright face is depth, precision and memory; his dark face is brooding and despair, the same weight turned inward until it stops producing anything. Autumn's deepening red is the arm of Passion on this dial, and Goethe's reading of that hue — light going down fighting — is the temperament stated as colour. "For in much wisdom is much grief" (Ecclesiastes 1:18).

His age is Middle Age — the turn of a life, when the harvest is counted and the evening first shows. His opposite across the wheel is the Sanguine (autumn against spring, heaviness against laughter, the evening of life against its morning), and spring's Renewal is the medicine for his brooding.

The Phlegmatic holds the winter arm because phlegm is cold and moist, and so is the year at its lowest. He is the Peacemaker, and the seat's claim is that endurance is an active virtue rather than the absence of one: his calm outlasts storms that heat cannot. His bright face is Serenity, endurance and mercy; his dark face is sloth, the calm that never moves at all and calls its refusal peace. Winter blue is Goethe's first colour of darkness and the Servant's own hue on this dial, which is the same disposition read from the roster instead of from the humors. "In quietness and in confidence shall be your strength" (Isaiah 30:15).

His age is Old Age — the still evening of a life, the water gone quiet. His total opposite is the Choleric at the top of the year (water against fire), and the summer's drive is what his stillness most lacks and most fears.

The Sanguine holds the spring arm because blood is warm and moist, the pairing the season itself carries. He is the Companion, and the seat argues that sociability is a temperament rather than a skill: he is everyone's friend within the hour because openness costs him nothing. His bright face is that openness and the joy that comes with it; his dark face is fickleness — he starts everything and finishes nothing, and promises faster than he can pay. Spring green is the Renewal arm of the whole wheel, which is why the lightest humor sits on the hour of beginning. "Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay" (James 5:12).

His age is Childhood and Youth — the morning of a life, all beginning and no ending yet. His opposite is the Melancholic across the dial (spring against autumn, the morning against the evening), and the Thinker's depth is exactly the ballast his lightness needs.

The centre is the Throne — the dual seat of the year, ruler and servant in one body. It is Goethe's two poles held together: the summer yellow above (the first color of light, the Ruler, the longest day) and the winter blue below (the first color of darkness, the Servant, the longest night), with the equinox green their exact union. On Sundays the Seasons light BOTH solstice arms — the two faces of one throne, a year apart and one dial tall. Its virtues are Justice and Humility, and "to every thing there is a season" (Ecclesiastes 3:1) is the law it keeps.

The Lion holds the summer arm of fire — the creature of Mark, whose gospel opens with a voice roaring in the wilderness. He is one of the four living creatures Ezekiel saw carrying the throne by the river Chebar, and one of the four that keep vigil around the throne in heaven "and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy" (Revelation 4:8). The Tetramorph does not act; it WITNESSES — the eighth archetype, the only one not human, a bestiary outside the seven the way the Ninths are outside the eights. In the older sky the Lion is Leo, the fixed sign of fire, our Choleric summer given a witness.

The Lion became Mark, and the assignment follows the gospel's own opening rather than any later convention. Mark begins with neither cradle nor genealogy but with a voice in the wilderness, and his is the shortest and fastest of the four — all urgency and action, set on the untamed ground where the Baptist cries out. The lion is the beast of exactly that ground: king of what is not cultivated, and therefore the witness that fits a gospel with no domestic prologue. The summer arm keeps him because fire and urgency are one disposition read in two registers. "The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord" (Mark 1:3).

Fire is the element the summer arm holds — hot and dry, the humor of yellow bile, the Choleric's own substance. On the Four Elements wheel it burns the classical flame-red, the scorched red of live coals kept deliberately apart from the temperament wheel's summer gold so the two cross readings never look alike. It is the element that drives and consumes, kin to the Commander's fire that can warm a house or burn it down; the Lion is its beast, and Leo, the fixed sign of fire, its place in the older sky.

The Ox holds the autumn arm of earth — the creature of Luke, whose gospel opens with a temple sacrifice, Zechariah at the altar. Patient under the yoke, he is the beast of labor and offering, the witness whose element is the soil itself. Among the four faces Ezekiel and John beheld, he is the strength that bows its neck; in the zodiac he is Taurus, the fixed sign of earth, our Melancholic autumn keeping vigil around the throne.

The Ox became Luke, and the assignment is made by his gospel's first office rather than by temperament. Luke opens in the Temple at the hour of incense, with Zechariah at the altar of sacrifice, so the evangelist's first subject is priesthood — and the ox is the animal of offering, the beast laid on that altar. His is the gospel of mercy and of the sacrifice that gives itself, which is the same argument the ox makes as a labouring animal: strength that bows its neck. The autumn arm keeps him because harvest and offering are one motion in an agricultural year. "There appeared unto him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense" (Luke 1:11).

Earth is the element the autumn arm holds — cold and dry, the humor of black bile, the Melancholic's own substance. On the wheel it wears an olive green-brown, the muddy green of turned soil, the heaviest and most inward of the four. It is the element of harvest and of weight, of depth bought with heaviness — the ground that holds both the grave and the seed. The Ox is its beast, patient under the yoke, and Taurus the fixed sign of earth keeping watch around the throne.

The Eagle holds the winter arm of water — the creature of John, whose gospel flies highest of the four: "In the beginning was the Word" (John 1:1). He is the far-seeing witness, the one who looks straight into the light without blinking. In the ancient sky his sign is Scorpio, whose nobler older symbol was the eagle, the fixed sign of water — our Phlegmatic winter lifted on wings around the throne.

The Eagle became John, and the assignment is the plainest of the four: his gospel does not begin on earth at all. Where the others open with a birth, a genealogy or a wilderness, John opens before creation — the eternal Word, a prologue no other evangelist attempts. The eagle is the creature the ancient tradition credited with gazing into the sun without blinking, which is precisely the claim that prologue makes about its own subject. The winter arm keeps him because water is the deep no wind troubles to the bottom, and John's is the gospel with the most bottom. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1).

Water is the element the winter arm holds — cold and moist, the humor of phlegm, the Phlegmatic's own substance. On the wheel it wears a deep water blue, the color of the frozen lake under the longest night and of the calm that outlasts every storm. It is the still, enduring element — serene at its best, slothful at its worst, the deep no wind can trouble to the bottom. The Eagle is its beast, and Scorpio, whose older nobler symbol was the eagle, its fixed sign of water.

The Man holds the spring arm of air — the creature of Matthew, whose gospel begins with Christ's human genealogy, the Word traced through generations of men. Named a winged man or an angel in the tradition, he is the witness wearing our own face among the beasts. In the zodiac he is Aquarius, the fixed sign of air — our Sanguine spring, the morning of the year, keeping vigil around the throne with the Lion, the Ox and the Eagle.

The Man became Matthew, and the assignment follows the genealogy his gospel opens with. Matthew begins with a ladder of names, tracing the Word down through the human generations into flesh, so his creature wears our own face — winged, because a witness at the throne is not merely a man. His is the gospel of descent into the family of man, which is why the fourth creature is the one that looks like the reader. The spring arm keeps him because air is the quickest and most open of the elements, and a genealogy is the year's own morning: everything that follows, prepared for. "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1).

Air is the element the spring arm holds — warm and moist, the humor of blood, the Sanguine's own substance. On the wheel it wears a pale white-yellow, the luminous lightest of the four, the near-weightless glass of a breeze full of light. It is the quickest and most moving element, the wind that lifts blossom and swallow at the morning of the year, open and changeable, settling nowhere for long. The Man is its beast — our own face among the creatures — and Aquarius the fixed sign of air.

The centre is the Throne — the dual seat of the year, ruler and servant in one body. It is Goethe's two poles held together: the summer yellow above (the first color of light, the Ruler, the longest day) and the winter blue below (the first color of darkness, the Servant, the longest night), with the equinox green their exact union. On Sundays the Seasons light BOTH solstice arms — the two faces of one throne, a year apart and one dial tall. Its virtues are Justice and Humility, and "to every thing there is a season" (Ecclesiastes 3:1) is the law it keeps.

The yellow summit belongs to The One — God, and the quality is LOVE: the shared summit where love of others (Weakness) and love of self (Pride) meet at the exact point they become sin. He is the union of the two natures the wheel splits below him, the apex of the triangle the banknote draws in G, M and N over the Eye. His diagonal is Love against Hatred — The One against the Devil at the bottom of the dial.

Love here is not the sentiment but the source: the thing every arm is a facet of, and the thing that at its extreme turns to sin. The One holds it whole where the others hold only a face of it — Courage a part, Humility a part, Pride and Fear its ruin. "God is love" (1 John 4:8), and the One is where that love is still undivided.

Michael the Archangel holds the orange arm of Zeal, and his quality is COURAGE. Revelation 12 holds the whole cast in one chapter: "there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon" (12:7), and the Accuser is thrown down (12:10). He balances the wheel three-and-three — The One, Jesus and Michael against Lucifer, the Devil and Judas.

Courage is the virtue that lies between despair and rage, and Michael's diagonal is Fear against Courage — the Archangel against Judas, the one who FIGHTS against the one who DESPAIRED. His is the fighting virtue turned to its right use: not the Wrath of the red arm but the sword raised for another.

Lucifer holds the red arm, and his quality is PRIDE — the sin of ascent rather than of appetite. The seat turns on direction: his one recorded ambition is not to destroy the throne but to occupy it, which makes him the pole of self-regard and not of malice. His whole regard is forward, entitled to a future he has not been given, and red is the arm the Triads already read as the future. His diagonal is Humility against Pride, and his fall is the measure of that whole axis. "I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God" (Isaiah 14:13).

Pride is Courage overreached, the virtue of the arm beside him turned to madness. His diagonal is Humility against Pride — Lucifer against Jesus, the one who wanted to ascend against the one who chose to descend: "whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased" (Luke 14:11). The cure he refused was Love-in-deed, given to others, now.

The bottom of the wheel, in purple Sorrow, belongs to The Devil, and his quality is HATRED — the shared ROOT of the virtue pair, not their summit. Turned inward it drags Humility down into the self-loathing of Judas; turned outward it turns Courage into Wrath, madness and overreach, the sin of Lucifer. Hatred is the poison that either extreme drinks.

His diagonal is Hatred against Love — the Devil against The One on the vertical axis, midnight against noon. Where the top holds love still undivided, the bottom holds its exact negation; the whole wheel turns on this axis, and every other person on it leans toward one pole or the other.

Judas holds the blue arm, and his quality is WEAKNESS — read here as Fear rather than as fragility. His fall is the refusal to believe that forgiveness extended to him, which is a judgment about his own worth and not about the offence: despair is self-regard inverted, not self-regard abandoned. Blue is the Triads' arm of the past, and his sin is the past made permanent, a mistake stared at until it becomes a grave. He is the shadow the blue arm always carries — the road from dwelling on what was to no longer moving at all. "Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself" (Matthew 27:3), and stopped there.

His diagonal is Fear against Courage — Judas against Michael, the one who despaired against the one who fought. The medicine was Hope, the cross-dial virtue he refused: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before" (Philippians 3:13). Fear is not cured by argument but by a courage borrowed from across the wheel.

Jesus holds the green arm of Renewal, and his quality is HUMILITY — renunciation, the same nature as his Trinity seat, love turned wholly toward others. He is the one who descended on purpose, the counterweight to Lucifer's climb: "he that humbleth himself shall be exalted" (Luke 14:11). Green is the arm of things made new, and Humility is the virtue that renews a soul from the root.

His diagonal is Humility against Pride — Jesus against Lucifer, the descent against the ascent. With the six persons seated, every diagonal becomes a person-pair, and this one is the sharpest: the same love, once bent toward the self and once poured out, once climbing and once bowing.

The Prism's centre is the Seal — the Banknote hexagram, and this wheel's claim that objectivity is a position rather than a virtue. Its six vertices carry six letters drawn from the Great Seal's mottos and coloured to this wheel, and they spell G and MASON: God crowning the whole, with MASON picked out of the letters as the folk reading of the dollar star has always done. Its two interlaced triangles are this canon's two doctrines — the Trinity in G, M and N (God, the Master, the Nazarene) and the Union in S, O and A (Sigma, Omega, Alpha), the court above and the alphabet of time below. Where each arm bends the light toward an office, the centre is the standard none of them owns, which is what the note's own motto says. "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending" (Revelation 1:8).

The top of the wheel, in green, is Gratitude — the highest and purest form of love, read as GROWTH: the answer that all giving quietly waits for. It is Jupiter's Generosity conjugated between two people, the virtue of the yellow seat spoken in the dual and worn in the light wheel's green. Where one gives and the other is truly thankful, the bond grows the way the green arm grows.

Its shadow is Taking for Granted — the giving received as if it were owed, the fastest way to starve a home. The cure lies across the wheel: Gratitude cures Score-keeping, and Tolerance cures Taking-for-granted — each diagonal healing the other, as the whole dial's cross-cures always do. "Love... beareth all things, believeth all things" (1 Corinthians 13:7).

The yellow arm of the daylight shoulder is Support — my Courage placed at your service, Mars's virtue conjugated into the bond. It is being someone's working light: to be beside them at the frontier of whatever they face, so that neither fights alone. In the light wheel it wears yellow, the color of the sun you become for another.

Its shadow is the Fight — Wrath between two, courage turned against the partner instead of the trouble. Its diagonal cure is Trust: Support cures Suspicion, and Trust disarms the Fight — the Moon and Mars axis spoken in the dual. "Two are better than one... for if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow" (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10).

On the red arm is Passion — love embodied, Venus's own virtue on Venus's own hue, needing no conjugation because it was always relational. It is the fire that keeps two people turned toward each other, the heat the whole bond banks against the cold. Red is where the light wheel burns hottest, and Passion is what it burns for.

Its shadow is Jealousy — the fire turned to suspicion of the other. Across the wheel Passion burns away Contempt and Respect calms Jealousy (the Venus and Saturn axis conjugated): the flame and the patience cure each other's excess. Love "envieth not" (1 Corinthians 13:4).

At the bottom, in magenta, is Tolerance — knowing the other is NOT you and never will be, and loving them anyway. It is Mercury's Wisdom conjugated, the midnight-talk virtue: two can never love and do all the same things, and Tolerance is the room a bond leaves for that difference. Understanding and empathy fold into it — the same target, one seat.

Its shadow is Score-keeping — keeping a ledger of who gave what, Mercury's Greed spoken in the dual. Its diagonal cure is Gratitude, and it in turn cures Taking-for-granted: the famous verse names it two thousand years early — love "keepeth no record of wrongs" (1 Corinthians 13:5).

On the blue arm of Calm is Trust — the relational face of honesty, the owner's own conjugation law: honesty is a trait of the individual, Trust its counterpart in the bond. It is the Moon's Serenity between two, calm BECAUSE of the other; the body's proof of it is sleeping soundly beside someone. Blue is the still, trusting hour of the dial, and Trust is what stills it.

Its shadow is Suspicion — Fear conjugated, the sentry who never leaves his post. Its diagonal cure is Support: Trust disarms the Fight and Support cures Suspicion. "Love... believeth all things" (1 Corinthians 13:7) — the bond's decision to credit the other before demanding proof.

On the cyan arm is Respect — what only years can build, Saturn's Patience conjugated, for Saturn IS time. It is the clear, cool air you leave around what you respect: respect keeps a clean distance, and cyan is that clear air made a color. The slowest pillar to raise and the surest once raised.

Its shadow is Contempt — the bond's deadliest poison, Envy soured into looking down. Across the wheel Respect calms Jealousy and Passion burns away Contempt: the patience and the fire trade cures. Love "is patient... it is not proud... it is not rude" (1 Corinthians 13:4-5) — the exact anatomy of a marriage read off the dial's geometry.

At the center is the Union — Zajednistvo, mutual servant-kingship: each RULES and SERVES the other, the throne's dual nature conjugated between two. Its two faces are Odanost, the day face (the union KEPT, the word held before the world) and Bliskost, the night face (the union FELT: the shared topics, the private world of two that exists nowhere else). Its shadow is tyranny of one or erasure of the other; its Ninth is the Child, the union made flesh, carrying the family circuit where everyone gives and everyone receives. "They shall be one flesh" (Genesis 2:24); "a threefold cord is not quickly broken" (Ecclesiastes 4:12) — and Aristotle, asked what a friend is: "one soul dwelling in two bodies."

The King holds noon, the throne hour, in royal gold — power at its zenith, the day at its height. The Walks are matter, and his matter is the crown's own metal: "by me kings reign, and princes decree justice" (Proverbs 8:15). Across the wheel his opposite is the Wanderer at midnight, the crown against the open road — Pride against Humility once more.

His object is the Crown — the circle of gold that says the power is the office, not the man. It is the noon arm's substance, brightest on the whole day-arc, and the estate every other Walk measures itself against.

The Merchant holds the afternoon because his estate's hour is the one in which exchange peaks and settles before dark. His substance is copper, the coin's own metal, and the Walks are a wheel of MATTER: every estate is argued from what it handles. Across the dial his opposite is the Scholar in the deep night, and the pairing states the oldest argument in economics — what a thing COSTS against what a thing is WORTH. The afternoon arm is therefore the seat of price, the public and loud scale, against the private and silent one at the far side.

His object is the Coin — copper struck round, the token that lets one good become any other. Where the Scholar weighs worth in silence, the Merchant weighs cost in the open, and the day needs both scales.

The Soldier holds the sunset arm because his estate exists at a threshold, and sunset is the day's own. His substance is iron in its crimson register — the metal of the weapon and of what the weapon costs — and his virtue is Courage with Wrath as its shadow, the pair a frontier forces a man to choose between. His opposite across the wheel is the Farmer at dawn, and the two are the same metal put to opposite work, which is why the prophets speak of converting one into the other rather than of abolishing it. "They shall beat their swords into plowshares" (Isaiah 2:4).
His object is the Sword — iron given an edge, the estate that holds the line at the border of the light. Courage is his virtue and Wrath his shadow, and the frontier is where both are decided.

The Artist holds the evening arm because performance is an after-dark estate: an audience exists only once the day's work has released it. His substance is velvet, the theatre's own material, and his object is the Mask — the seat's whole argument, since a mask is the instrument by which a truth the bare face cannot say is said. His opposite across the wheel is the Priest in the morning, and the pairing is exact rather than ironic: both estates perform toward something past this world, one addressing the crowd and one addressing heaven.
His object is the Mask — the face put on to tell a truth the bare face cannot. Velvet is his substance, the evening arm's own dark richness, and the Mask is how the Artist makes the many feel as one.

The Wanderer holds midnight because his estate is defined by having no place, and midnight is the hour with the fewest. His substance is road dust, the darkest register of the whole day-arc, and the Norse dual already walks this hour under the same name. His opposite is the King at noon, and the pairing is the Walks' sharpest: the man who holds everything against the man who has let everything go — the Self-Regard axis of the Cube, and what this canon has always read as Pride against Humility.

His object is the Staff — the one possession of the one who possesses nothing, the walking-stick that is road and roof and weapon at once. His substance is the dust of the road itself, worn into the color of the deep night he crosses.

The Scholar holds the deep night because his estate keeps an hour no other estate wants. His substance is ink and his object the Book, and the argument is that worth, unlike price, is established in silence and over time. His opposite across the wheel is the Merchant in the crowded afternoon: the quiet ledger against the loud one, worth against cost. The seat trades the sleep of the body for the waking of the mind, which is the exact expense that defines the estate.
His object is the Book — the lamp-blued page where worth is weighed in silence. His is the hour no one else keeps, and the estate that trades the sleep of the body for the waking of the mind.

The Farmer holds the dawn arm because his work is bound to first light and because his virtue is the one that waits. His substance is field green, the growing colour on the growing hour, and his object is the Plough — iron turned to feeding rather than to fighting. His opposite across the wheel is the Soldier at sunset, and the two share the same metal: one opens the ground the other only defends. Patience is his virtue in the strict sense, since he sows and cannot shorten the interval. "The husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it" (James 5:7).

His object is the Plough — iron turned to feeding instead of fighting, the tool that opens the ground the Soldier only defends. Patience is his virtue: he sows and WAITS, and the green arm is the reward of that waiting.

The Priest holds the morning because his estate's hours are the ones that begin things: the mass and the school bell ring at the same end of the day. His substance is ivory, the pale linen register of the morning arm, and his object is the Bell — the estate that speaks before a word is said, gathering a town by sound alone. His opposite across the wheel is the Artist in the evening, and the pairing argues that teaching and performance are one act aimed differently: one calls the many toward heaven, the other toward the play.

His object is the Bell — rung for mass and for school alike, the sound that gathers the town at the day's beginning. Ivory is his substance, the pale linen of the morning arm, and the Bell is how the estate of teaching speaks before a word is said.

At noon, the zenith, is Youth in sun-yellow — life at its blazing height, the noon of a man read onto the noon of the sky. No age fits the top of the wheel better than the one that owns strength before the descent. Shakespeare gave the world seven ages of man ("all the world's a stage", As You Like It); this wheel gives his stage an eighth player, and Youth is the one the whole crowd watches.

In the afternoon, in amber, is Maturity — the yoke years, the full green of Youth deepened into fruit-bearing strength. The blaze of noon has steadied into work that lasts; the light has begun, almost unnoticed, to lean toward evening. Amber is the day-arc's turn from gold toward ember, the hour a life stops climbing and starts building.

At sunset, in ember, is the Elder — the harvest of a life, when what was sown across the whole day is finally counted. His is the fruit-laden hour, memory and authority ripened to their fullest before the dark. Ember is the sunset arm's own color, the light richest just as it begins to go — the gathered warmth of everything the day has been.

In the evening, in dusk violet, is Old Age — the leaf-fall, the slow letting-go after the harvest is in. The colors cool; the day's work is done and the long quiet begins. Violet is the twilight arm, purple's gentle light, the hour a life turns from doing toward watching.

At midnight, in pure white, is Death — and in the light register death goes INTO the light, not out of it. "A time to be born, and a time to die" (Ecclesiastes 3:2); the Serbian tongue says a dying man PREDADE DUH, surrendered the spirit — Christ's own word on the cross, "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit" (Luke 23:46). White is the sum of all colors and the color of the swan's last song; the arm that looks darkest on the paint wheel here burns brightest.

Before dawn, in moonlight silver, is the Unborn — and this wedge holds TWO peoples at once: the ancestors who have passed and the not-yet-born who wait, one moonlight pool of souls. It is the community of souls a life returns to and comes from, the seed in the dark soil and the phoenix in the ash. Here the wheel is about to close and open again — NOVUS ORDO SECLORUM enacted on the dial, the order of the ages born anew with every turn.

Birth holds the first-light arm because the Ages wheel maps a life onto a day, and a life's first act is arrival rather than growth. Its hue is the pale grey-blue of the moment before colour: life present before it has a quality of its own, which is the exact claim the age makes. It follows Death and the Unborn on the wheel rather than opening it, and that ordering is the light register's argument — the circle closes in silver and white and opens again here, so birth is a continuation and not a beginning. "Naked came I out of my mother's womb" (Job 1:21).

In the morning, in spring green, is Childhood — the sapling, the swallow, the growing thing on the growing hour. The mist of birth has burned off into the clear green of a day just begun; everything is reaching upward and nothing yet has weight. Green is the Renewal arm's own promise, and Childhood is the age that keeps it.

sun.name: Antarctica · Arctic
sun.base:
[[The Figure]] The Sunday center of the Continents is the pair of poles — the two ends of the axis the whole dial turns on, held as one dual body the way every theme's throne holds a Ruler and a Servant. They look like twins and they are opposites: one is a true continent of rock and mountain buried under ice, the other is only ocean that has frozen over. Reality and its reflection, the land and the mirror of the land, seated together at the still point of the wheel.

[[On the Dial]] On the hexa and trio pointers the poles take no arm — they hold the center, like every reading of the throne. The face follows the live sky and the chosen style; near solar noon the Ruler shines, near solar midnight the Servant takes the seat, the two trading places by the same solar law the whole center obeys.

[[The Two Faces]] The poles are the theme's dual law made planetary. They live in eternal antiphase: when it is polar day at one it is polar night at the other, six months of sun answered by six months of dark, always exactly opposed. That is the Ruler-and-Servant solar window written across the whole planet — not a metaphor for the antiphase but the thing itself. The bright face and the dark face of one axis, forever taking turns.

faces.ruler: Antarctica is the Ruler — the true continent, and the only one on the dial that earns the throne by simple fact: under the two miles of ice there is real rock, mountains and a buried coastline, a genuine seventh continent with land beneath. It is the highest, driest, coldest, emptiest of them all, ruled by no nation and reserved by treaty for science and peace — a throne held in trust rather than by conquest, which is the only kind of throne this dial has ever honored. It keeps the seat near solar noon, the Ruler's own hour, the real land at the bright end of the axis.
faces.servant: The Arctic is the Servant — and its whole nature is that it is not a continent. It is an ocean with a lid: sea ice you can walk across, a floor of frozen water with no land beneath, the convincing image of a pole that is really the sea wearing the shape of one. That is the Servant's truth in every theme — the reflection that serves the real, the mirror that shows the throne without being it. It takes the center near solar midnight, the dark end of the axis, in eternal antiphase to the true land at the top of the world — reality and its shadow, forever trading the light between them.

variants.hexa_primary: The poles hold the center on the hexa dial, no arm — the still point the whole wheel turns on, Antarctica near solar noon and the Arctic near solar midnight, the Ruler and the Servant trading the seat by the sun.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette the center is unchanged — the poles keep the throne in both wheels, the axis the dial spins on caring nothing for paint or light, only for noon and midnight.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass the poles take the 12h King arm in royal gold (#F0C420), the throne hour — Antarctica the crowned continent, the true land ruling from the top of the wheel, the Arctic its servant-mirror at the year's other end.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel the 12h arm is Youth in sun yellow (#FFE800), the zenith of a life — the poles wear it as the newest-known ground on Earth, the last continent found, young to us however old the ice.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross the poles share the 12h summer arm with Africa — the ends of the axis beside the cradle at the top of the year, the coldest ground on the warmest arm, the throne and the source together at noon.
variants.trio: On the Trinity the poles hold the center, the throne above the three arms — Antarctica the Ruler and the Arctic the Servant, the oldest dual on the dial made of ice: the real land and the frozen sea that mirrors it.

moon.name: Oceania
moon.base:
[[The Figure]] Oceania is less a continent than a scattering — Australia's great red island and ten thousand smaller ones flung across a third of the planet's water, the one weekday body that is mostly ocean. It is the Moon's own country: the same body that pulls the tides governs a world where the tide is the loudest event of the day and the reef breathes with it. Few people live here by the standards of the crowded north; the distances are enormous and the calm is real — island time, the unhurried Serenity of a place the sea keeps at arm's length from the rest of the world.

[[On the Dial]] Monday's diamond rides the 4h arm at the dial's lower left in deep blue, the Moon's hour, the cool quarter before dawn where the water is stillest. The face turns with the sky the whole instrument reads — the atmosphere globe or the clean one as the user has set it, lit or dark as the real sun stands over the observer — so Oceania on the dial is always the Oceania of this hour, never a postcard.

[[The Two Faces]] The Moon's virtue is Serenity and its vice is Fear, and they are the same sensitivity read twice — the calm surface that feels every tremor is the nerve that startles at every shadow. Oceania gives that Fear a literal face no other continent can match: it is home to the most lethal fauna alive — the saltwater crocodile, the great white, the taipan and the box jellyfish, the funnel-web spider, a bestiary of the world's deadliest venoms gathered under one serene blue sky. The paradise and the danger are one place, exactly as Serenity and Fear are one nerve.

[[The Physician]] And the physician cell — Monday's own profession — closes the circle the way medicine always answers fear: the land of the world's worst venoms is the world's capital of antivenom. Australia built the science of it, the sera that turn a taipan bite from a death sentence into a hospital afternoon. Fear named the poison; the Physician answered with the cure drawn from the poison itself. Serenity is not the absence of the deadly thing — it is the antivenom in the cabinet.

variants.hexa_primary: Home position: the 4h arm at the dial's lower left in deep blue (#002FFF), the Moon's cool quarter before dawn — the hour the tide runs stillest, the base article's own island calm.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette the arm stays at 4h and stays blue (#0040FF) — the Moon keeps its water-hue in both wheels, the one body whose color never flinches between paint and light, fitting for the continent that is mostly sea.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass Oceania lands on the 3h Scholar arm in lamp-ink blue (#1F5FA8), the lone student awake with the stars — a fair seat for the reef biologist and the venom researcher, the patient night-watch science that turns a taipan into a treatable bite.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel that 3h arm is the Unborn in moonlight silver (#C8D7F0), the ancestors and the not-yet-born held in one pool. Oceania wears it well: the oldest continuous cultures on Earth live here, and the reef itself is a nursery, life not yet arrived.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross Oceania takes the 6h spring arm, green for the year's morning, sharing it with Saturn's harvest — the Moon's water beside Saturn's soil, tide and field, the two quiet providers on the dawn side of the wheel.
variants.trio: The Trinity moves Oceania to the 4h Hope arm, blue, beside Mercury — Hope reads through the physician here: the antivenom in the cabinet is hope made chemical, the calm that comes not from the absence of the deadly thing but from the cure kept ready for it.

mars.name: Europe
mars.base:
[[The Figure]] Europe is small — a crowded western cape of the Asian landmass — and it changed the whole planet more than any land its size has a right to. It is Mars' continent, and its defining century is the one when it built the caravel: a ship a few dozen meters long, cramped and leaking, and sailed it off the edge of every map it had into a world it did not know existed. That is Courage in its purest form — not standing your ground but leaving it, betting your life on the guess that the sea comes back to land.

[[On the Dial]] Tuesday's diamond rides the 16h arm at the upper right in ember orange, the working afternoon the mood-wheel calls Zeal — the banked fire of effort, exactly the heat that drives a crew across an ocean. The face follows the live sky and the user's chosen style, so Europe on the dial burns in the real light of its own hour.

[[The Two Faces]] Mars' virtue is Courage and its vice is Wrath, and the deepest beauty of this whole theme is that they are not two things but one — the daring that discovers is the daring that conquers. The same sails that found the new coasts came back carrying cannon; the same restless nerve that crossed the Atlantic crossed its own borders for a thousand years of wars and ended, twice in one century, in world war. Europe did not have a courageous half and a wrathful half. It had one fire, and it pointed the fire outward as discovery and inward as slaughter, often in the same decade, often on the same ships.

[[The Soldier]] Tuesday's profession is the Soldier, and Europe is his continent by right: the estate whose whole art is the disciplined application of force, glorious when it holds a frontier and monstrous when it makes one. The vice is written plainly and at the system, never at a people — the conquests were carried outward, the wars exported to every coast the caravels reached, so that Europe's Wrath became the world's wound. Courage and Wrath: the sail that discovers and the sail that brings the guns, one mast, one wind.

variants.hexa_primary: Home position: the 16h arm at the upper right in ember orange (#DC9600), the Zeal of the working afternoon — the banked fire that drives a crew across an ocean, the base article's own daring.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette the arm stays at 16h but the ember flares to pure yellow (#FFFF00) — pigment's orange has no seat in the prism wheel, so Europe's afternoon fire burns at light's brightest hue instead. Zeal, only hotter.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass Europe lands on the 15h Merchant arm in copper (#C87533), the Coin for its object — apt for the continent that turned discovery into the trading empires, the caravel's courage cashed out as cargo and colony.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel that 15h arm is Maturity in amber (#FFB400), the prime of a life, strength that knows its own reach — Europe wears it as the age of confidence that built and conquered in one breath, courage seasoned and, too often, overreaching.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross Europe takes the 18h autumn arm, red, sharing it with Venus — the warrior beside the lover on the year's evening, Mars and Venus in their oldest pairing, the continent of the caravel beside the continent of the carnival.
variants.trio: The Trinity moves Europe to the 20h Love arm, red, beside Venus — and Love reads through Mars here as the terrible closeness of the virtue and the vice: the fierce devotion that defends a home is the same fire that, turned outward, burns a stranger's.

mercury.name: Asia
mercury.base:
[[The Figure]] Asia is the great body of the world — most of its land, most of its people, and the road that tied the rest together. Its defining thing is not a border but a route: the Silk Road, four thousand miles of merchants, messengers and translators moving silk and spice, script and number, gods and gunpowder between civilizations that would otherwise never have touched. That is Mercury's own profession made continental — the merchant, the go-between, the one who carries.

[[On the Dial]] Wednesday's diamond sits at the dial's bottom, the 24h region, in Mercury's deep purple — the crossroads hour the mood-wheel calls Sorrow, the long road's own melancholy of wisdom, the still point where the day's traffic turns over. The globe follows the live sky and the chosen style, Asia lit or dark as the real sun stands, always the hour's own face.

[[The Two Faces]] Mercury's virtue is Wisdom and its vice is Greed, and again they are one force, not two: knowledge and trade are the same act of exchange, and the same road that carried the wisdom carried the appetite. Asia's Wisdom is the actual cargo of the Silk Road — the philosophies and religions, the alphabets, the zero and the decimal, paper and the compass, everything the caravans taught the world as they passed. Its Greed is the shadow of the identical trade: the silk and spice monopolies fought over for centuries and, at the bitter end, the Opium Wars — commerce turned into a weapon, a whole nation drugged for a trade balance.

[[The Merchant]] Wednesday's profession is the Merchant, and the vice belongs to the system of the trade, never to the trader as a soul — a road built to move value will, unwatched, move poison for profit as readily as wisdom for wonder; the two ran the same rails. Asia is the continent where the ledger and the sutra travelled in the same saddlebag, where the merchant's Wisdom and the merchant's Greed were the going and the coming of a single caravan.

variants.hexa_primary: Home position: the 24h arm at the dial's bottom in deep purple (#542E85), Mercury's crossroads hour — the still point where the world's traffic turns over, the base article's own road.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette the arm stays at the bottom but purple flares to magenta (#BD00BD) — the prism's own crossing hue, fitting for the continent that is one vast crossing, every road meeting every other.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass Asia lands on the 21h Artist arm in stage-velvet violet (#7A2E8E) — a fair seat for the continent that gave the world its scripts and silks, the merchant's road doubling as the longest gallery in history, wisdom carried as beautiful things.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel that 21h arm is Old age in dusk violet (#9C6BD4) — and no continent wears it more truly: Asia holds the oldest living civilizations, the deep memory of the species, the merchant grown into the sage the whole caravan once set out to become.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross Asia takes the 24h winter arm alone, blue, the year's midnight — Wednesday's lone seat, the still deep of the wheel where the crossroads rests and the long roads wait out the cold.
variants.trio: The Trinity moves Asia to the 4h Hope arm, blue, beside the Moon — Hope reads through the merchant as the promise every exchange holds: the road that carries wisdom is the road that carries the future, one caravan at a time.

jupiter.name: Africa
jupiter.base:
[[The Figure]] Africa is where we begin — the cradle of the whole species, the ground every human family tree climbs down to. It is Jupiter's continent, the king-planet's own abundance made land: the great herds and the last true megafauna, the river valleys, the oldest sunlight on the oldest rock. And it is mankind's first teacher — the griot, the keeper of the spoken library who holds a village's whole history in memory and sings it forward, the oldest form of the school there is, older than writing.

[[On the Dial]] Thursday's diamond rides the top of the dial, the noon arm, in Jupiter's warm yellow — the high, generous light of the day at its fullest, the mood the wheel calls Joy: the sheer joy of life's abundance. The globe turns with the live sky and the chosen style; Africa at the top of the wheel is the source at the top of the day.

[[The Two Faces]] Jupiter's virtue is Generosity and its vice is Excess, and here the theme does something it does nowhere else: the Excess is not chiefly Africa's own. Africa symbolizes the abundance of natural wealth — the land that gives. The shadow of that abundance lies not primarily in Africa itself but in the world's excessive taking from it: Jupiter's overflow of life becomes Jupiter's Excess as immoderate extraction, the rest of the world drawing more from the source that feeds it than the source was ever asked to give. The virtue is the land that gives; the vice is the world that takes too much.

[[The Teacher]] Thursday's profession is the Priest and the Teacher, and Africa holds it by the oldest right — the griot, the first teacher, the mother continent that taught the species to speak and remember before it taught it anything else. The lesson written here is the theme's second law: a shadow can live in the relationship between an archetype and the world, not only inside the archetype. Africa's Generosity is entire and its own; the Excess is a wound done to it, named plainly and at the system — the immoderate taking from the source — because naming it honestly is the first move of Renewal, the green return the mother continent has always modeled and always survived.

variants.hexa_primary: Home position: the 12h arm at the top of the dial in warm yellow (#F8E600), Jupiter's noon — the high generous light of the day at its fullest, the source at the top of the wheel.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette the top arm turns green (#00DC00) — growth itself, the additive wheel's spring hue. Africa wears it truly: the cradle that grew the species, Generosity shown not as gold but as living green.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass Africa lands on the 9h Priest arm in alb ivory (#EDEDE0), the teacher's morning hour — the exact estate of the griot, the first teacher, the mother continent seated where the school bell rings.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel that 9h arm is Childhood in spring green (#7CE577) — the beginning of a life on the continent that is the beginning of all our lives, the cradle wearing the color of the young.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross Africa takes the 12h summer arm, yellow, the year's high noon, sharing it with the Sun — the source of life beside the source of light, abundance and the star that feeds it on the top arm together.
variants.trio: The Trinity moves Africa to the 12h Faith arm, yellow, beside Saturn — Faith reads through the teacher here: the griot's whole craft is the faith that what is remembered and sung forward will outlast the one who carries it.

venus.name: South America
venus.base:
[[The Figure]] South America is the continent that turned life into rhythm. It is Venus' country — not the Venus of quiet beauty but of heat and music and the body in motion: the carnival that stops a nation, the samba and the tango and the drum that runs under everything, the tropical fertility of the Amazon pouring green out of the equator. Its red is not the red of war. It is the red of blood as life — the pulse, the flush of the dance, the warm arterial red of a continent that feels first and thinks after.

[[On the Dial]] Friday's diamond rides the 20h arm at the lower right in Venus' red, the evening the mood-wheel calls Passion — the hour the day softens into music and the feast begins. The globe turns with the live sky and the chosen style, South America lit or dark in the light of its own hour.

[[The Two Faces]] Venus' virtue is Love and its vice is Jealousy, and they are the one flame read twice — the ardor that gives itself wholly is the ardor that cannot bear to share. The same heat that makes the carnival makes the crime of passion; the same devotion that pours into a lover, a team, a saint's-day procession curdles the instant it turns possessive. South America does not love in half-measures, and so it does not envy in half-measures either — Jealousy here is simply Love that has stopped being able to let the beloved go.

[[The Artist]] Friday's profession is the Artist, and no continent holds it more completely: the whole of South American genius runs through color, music, dance and image — the mural, the bossa nova, the poem, the shirt of a national team worn like a vestment. The Artist's virtue and vice are Venus' own, named plainly: the Love that creates and the Jealousy that consumes are the same red heat, the same Passion, pointed toward the canvas or pointed toward the rival.

variants.hexa_primary: Home position: the 20h arm at the lower right in deep red (#B60000), Venus' evening — the hour the day softens into music and the feast begins, the base article's own Passion.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette the arm stays at 20h and stays red (#FF0000) — Venus keeps her heat in both wheels, the color of blood-as-life unchanged, the pulse under the carnival that never cools.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass South America lands on the 18h Soldier arm in iron-blood crimson (#A02020) — a hard seat for the continent of the dance, until the red is read honestly: the same arterial color serves the frontier and the festival, blood spilled and blood dancing, one hue.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel that 18h arm is the Elder in ember (#FF6A3C), the harvest of a life, the warm low sun — South America wears it as the deep old cultures under the new rhythm: the Inca terrace beneath the carnival, memory glowing under the music.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross South America takes the 18h autumn arm, red, sharing it with Mars — the lover beside the warrior on the year's evening, Venus and Mars again, the carnival's red beside the caravel's, feeling beside daring.
variants.trio: The Trinity moves South America to the 20h Love arm, red, beside Mars — its native seat: Love here is the whole continent's first language, the Passion that makes the art and, turned possessive, the Jealousy that is only Love unable to let go.

saturn.name: North America
saturn.base:
[[The Figure]] North America is the continent of the long work and the fresh start. It is Saturn's country — the old planet of time, patience and the harvest — and it wears the crown of the farmer: the Corn Belt and the Wheat Belt, the vast plains and forests that feed a large share of the world, one of the greatest agricultural engines the planet has. Its other name is the New World, and it means it: a land built by immigrants, a place people cross an ocean to begin again, where the past is something you are allowed to leave on the far shore.

[[On the Dial]] Saturday's diamond rides the 8h arm at the upper left in Saturn's green — the growing color, the morning of the working week, the field at first light. The globe turns with the live sky and the chosen style, North America in the true light of its own hour.

[[The Two Faces]] Saturn's virtue is Patience and its vice is Envy, and they are the one long habit read twice — the discipline of waiting is inseparable from the discipline of comparing, and a person who watches a crop grow for a season is a person who watches the neighbor's crop too. North America's Patience is the pioneer's: the fence line and the furrow, the slow taming of a wilderness, the multi-generational build of a nation out of raw land. Its Envy is the shadow that same measuring throws — the American Dream is a promise you can rise, and a promise you can rise is a machine that runs on comparison.

[[The Farmer]] Saturday's profession is the Farmer, and the vice belongs to the system, plainly named: a society that strongly rewards material success breeds Envy as its dominant shadow — the dream held up beside extreme inequality, the neighbor's yield always in view. Yet Saturn's mood is Renewal, and it is the glue of the whole wheel: the New World's genius is the reset, the immigrant's second chance, the field plowed under to be sown again. Patience builds the farm; Envy is the price of measuring it against the next farm; Renewal is the seed that closes the season and opens the next.

variants.hexa_primary: Home position: the 8h arm at the upper left in green (#007E00), Saturn's morning — the growing color, the field at first light, the base article's own patient work.
variants.hexa_secondary: In the light palette the 8h arm turns cyan (#00DDDD) — the clear cool air of the morning, the distance a patient farmer reads the weather across. Saturn's green cools to the horizon it plans against.
variants.octa_primary: On the Compass North America lands on the 6h Farmer arm in field green (#3E8914) — its own estate exactly, the plough in hand at dawn: no continent sits more squarely on its own profession than the New World on the Farmer.
variants.octa_secondary: In the Ages wheel that 6h arm is Birth in predawn mist (#8FA8C8) — the first light of a life, fitting for the continent whose whole promise is beginning again, the immigrant's dawn, the New World waking.
variants.cross: On the seasons cross North America takes the 6h spring arm, green, the year's morning, sharing it with the Moon — Saturn's field beside the Moon's tide, the two quiet providers, soil and water, on the dawn side of the wheel.
variants.trio: The Trinity moves North America to the 12h Faith arm, yellow, beside Jupiter — Faith reads through the farmer as the oldest faith there is: burying the seed in the dark and trusting the season, the patience that is faith with dirt on its hands.

rows: God holds midnight on the creation triangle because making, unlike judging, is not an act performed in the light. The Court reads the upward triangle — Judge at noon, Advocate at 04h, Prosecutor at 20h; the Genesis wheel reads its exact counter-triangle, and of the three persons only God keeps a full diameter, holding both ends of the 12-24 line the Banknote already reads as G against Omega. His creation arm is the purple-gray of the Judgment axis' negative pole, Integrity — the law that holds to the last — the moon hue of midnight and of the Winter Solstice, the hour at which the year itself is remade. The Court names him The One and this wheel names him God: the names are layered rather than reconciled, because a plurality of names presents him as more than a single personality. "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending" (Revelation 1:8).

As Creator he holds the office that acts on what the Court has already decided deserves to exist: judgment precedes transformation, and the inverted triangle is what follows the verdict. Creation is seated at the darkest hour because the first act recorded of it is performed over an unlit deep — the making is prior to the light, not a consequence of it. The Path of Light terminates on this same arm for the same reason: a road that ends in the Creator's hands ends remade rather than acquitted, "a new creature" (2 Corinthians 5:17). His diagonal partner is the Devil as Destroyer — making against unmaking on one line — while his own opposite hour holds his other office, the Judge. "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth" (Genesis 1:1).

Jesus holds the green arm of the creation triangle as the person whose whole work is to keep what has been made. Green is the negative pole of the Self-Regard axis, Humility — not self-contempt but the correct estimate of one's own weight — and preservation is that estimate applied to the world, an office that adds nothing of its own. The Banknote seats Alpha here, the beginning and the seed that falls into the ground (John 12:24), so the arm that keeps is also the arm that starts. On the Court he is the Advocate, who defends deeds already done; here he defends the made thing itself, which is one nature read twice: renunciation as pleading, renunciation as keeping. "He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it" (Matthew 10:39).

As Preserver he is the office set between creation and destruction, and it refuses to become either. The Genesis wheel is a balance rather than a sequence: what God makes and the Devil unmakes, Jesus holds, and a creation wheel with a maker and an unmaker but no keeper would be a triangle missing a side. His diagonal crosses to the Devil's Prosecutor — accusation against keeping, the charge laid against the thing that survives it. The same arm carries Hope as the first station of the Path of Light, the smallest living thing kept alive through the night. "Upholding all things by the word of his power" (Hebrews 1:3).

The Devil wears orange on the creation triangle and red on the Court, and the two colors are two offices rather than two persons. Orange is the positive pole of the Activation axis — Vigor, whose fall is Frenzy — so the Destroyer is the Devil read as force rather than as malice. The color-fidelity law permits a figure many faces provided each face is argued: as Prosecutor he is the red of accusation, as Destroyer the orange of the deed that ends things. Destruction on this wheel is an office and not a verdict — it is what makes room, and a world without it could only accumulate. "A time to break down, and a time to build up" (Ecclesiastes 3:3).

As Destroyer he supplies the creation triangle's necessary third motion: make, keep, unmake. The Double Trinity's order binds him — the Court decides what deserves to remain, and only then does the Destroyer act; unmaking that runs ahead of the verdict is Frenzy, the fall of his own color. His diagonal reaches Jesus as Advocate: defense against unmaking, the two offices that argue over the same object. The same arm carries Love as a station of the Path of Light, which is the identical vigor spent for another rather than against him. "Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth" (Hebrews 12:6).

The Beginning is the Genesis wheel's center because a creation triangle needs an origin rather than a witness. The Court's center watches — Providence attending to what already exists — while the creation wheel's center is the first act itself, the light called out over a deep that has nothing in it yet to be watched. The two centers therefore answer each other on one axis of meaning: the Eye is the seat of a case being heard, the Beginning the moment before there is a case to answer. Its hour is midnight, the Creator's own seat, which is why the Path of Light ends here remade rather than acquitted. "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light" (Genesis 1:3).

The Council seats three persons in six offices, and God's first seat is noon. The wheel is the two triangles interlocked — the Court's 12-04-20 and Genesis' 24-16-08 — so that judgment and creation are in session at once; the hexagram is the argument's own diagram rather than its decoration. Yellow is the positive pole of the Judgment axis, Loyalty: covenant kept, the basis of judgment that binds a judge to those he judges. The Court says The One where this wheel says God, and the difference is kept on purpose. "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods" (Psalm 82:1).

As Judge he holds the office the Council convenes around, since judgment precedes transformation and the noon seat opens the session. He is fit to weigh the case because he alone holds a full diameter — Judge at noon, Creator at midnight — and a judge who also makes cannot disown what he sentences. His hour is the present, the only seat from which a case can be heard at all: the Advocate works in the past and the Prosecutor strikes at the future. The Path of Darkness ends on this arm for the same reason — what fermented in the dark is exposed before the Judge at noon. "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" (Genesis 18:25).

The Devil sits twice in the Council, and orange is his creation seat. Orange is Vigor, the positive pole of the Activation axis, and it carries him as force rather than as accusation — the same person the red arm seats as Prosecutor. One person holding two offices is the Council's whole structure and not an inconsistency: six seats are three persons doubled, and the doubling is what closes the star. His diagonal runs to Jesus the Advocate, unmaking against defense. "A time to rend, and a time to sew" (Ecclesiastes 3:7).

As Destroyer his office is to execute what the Court has already decided, which is why the creation triangle is drawn beneath the judicial one. Destruction that waits for a verdict is an office; destruction that runs ahead of it is Frenzy, the fall of his own arm's virtue. In session he is the motion no council can delegate: a body that can only create and preserve accumulates until it collapses under its own weight. "To every thing there is a season... a time to kill, and a time to heal" (Ecclesiastes 3:1-3).

Red seats the Devil as Prosecutor, the office the scriptures name for him most often. KATEGOROS, the accuser of the brethren (Revelation 12:10), is the adversary who walks the earth in Job and accuses at Joshua's right hand in Zechariah 3; the Council gives that role a chair rather than a shadow. Red is the positive pole of the Self-Regard axis, Dignity, whose fall is Self-Worship: the prosecutor's virtue is that he holds the law's worth, his fall that he comes to hold his own. His other seat is orange, the Destroyer, and the Council never merges the two. "Then Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel" (1 Chronicles 21:1).

As Prosecutor he is the office that makes the Council a court rather than a committee. An accusation is the only instrument that forces a case to be heard: without it the Judge has nothing to weigh and the Advocate nothing to answer. He strikes forward, because an accusation is always about what the accused would go on to be, which is why the Triads read his arm as the future. His diagonal reaches Jesus the Preserver — the charge laid against the thing that survives it. "The accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night" (Revelation 12:10).

God's second seat is midnight, and it is the reason the vertical belongs to him alone. Purple-gray is the negative pole of the Judgment axis, Integrity — the law that holds to the last, "one jot or one tittle" (Matthew 5:18) — so the Council makes the same person the covenant at noon and the law at midnight. Jesus and the Devil hold diagonals; only God holds a diameter, and it is the Banknote's own G against Omega, beginning against end. Revelation 1:8 states that pair as an identity rather than as an opposition, which is exactly what the vertical claims.

As Creator he acts after judgment and never before it: the Council's order is judgment, then transformation. Creation is seated at the darkest hour of the day and of the year because making precedes light rather than following it. In session his creating answers his own judging across the dial — the person who decides what deserves to remain is the person who must then make what replaces what did not. "Behold, I make all things new" (Revelation 21:5).

Jesus takes the blue arm as Advocate, and blue is Composure, the negative pole of the Activation axis — the stilled storm and the accepted cup. PARAKLETOS (1 John 2:1) means literally the one called to stand beside; the office is defined by proximity to the accused rather than by eloquence. He works in the past, because a defense pleads deeds already done, and the Triads read blue as the arm of the past. His fall is Lethargy, the sleeping watch — the advocate who does not stay awake for his client. "If any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous" (1 John 2:1).

As Advocate his office answers the Prosecutor without becoming him: the Council balances not by moderating the accusation but by seating its opposite. His diagonal runs to the Devil as Destroyer — defense against unmaking, the sharper of the two crossings, since a defense that fails is not merely lost but undone. Composure is the virtue the office requires, for an advocate who matches the prosecutor's zeal has changed sides in temperament if not in argument. "Peace, be still" (Mark 4:39).

Green seats Jesus as Preserver, his second office and the humble pole of the Self-Regard axis. Humility here is accuracy rather than self-erasure, and preservation is that accuracy applied to the world: the office adds nothing of its own. The Banknote's Alpha sits on this arm — the beginning, the seed that falls into the ground (John 12:24) — so the seat that keeps is also the seat that starts. His other office is blue, the Advocate; the Council keeps them apart because defending a case and keeping a creation are different labors. "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus... he humbled himself" (Philippians 2:5-8).

As Preserver he gives the Council its stability: between a Creator and a Destroyer the wheel needs one seat whose entire work is continuance. His diagonal reaches the Prosecutor — accusation against keeping — and that crossing states the Council's deepest tension, since everything that endures endures under charge. The same arm holds Hope as the Path of Light's first station, for the identical reason: hope is the smallest living thing kept alive. "He that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved" (Matthew 24:13).

The Lord's Day is the Council's center because six offices in session require a seventh seat that does nothing. The six arms read as the six days of work — three judicial, three creative — and the middle is the rest that completes them; a week without its seventh day is not a shorter week but an unfinished one. The center is therefore a state and not an office: the only seat on the wheel defined by cessation. It answers its two siblings on the same axis of meaning — the Court's Eye watches, the Genesis Beginning starts, the Lord's Day stops. "And he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made" (Genesis 2:2).

Loyalty is the positive pole of the Judgment axis: judgment that rests on bonds rather than on rules. The Character wheel is the Cube with its depth axis set to zero — Activation is the one dimension a flat dial cannot show — so the compass reads Judgment against Self-Regard only, and yellow crowns it at noon as the covenant color, the God who says "I will be your God, and ye shall be my people". Its figures are Penelope in the archetypal set, Ernest Shackleton in the historical and Samwise Gamgee in the modern: three refusals to abandon, measured in years rather than in gestures. The seat binds to yellow's established readings on this dial — the arm of Joy, the Judge's own color, the Banknote's G — because a bond kept is the oldest basis anyone has had for weighing a case. "Whither thou goest, I will go... thy people shall be my people" (Ruth 1:16).

Tribalism is Loyalty walked past its measure: the bond kept so completely that it becomes the only law. The fall is not the loss of the covenant but its closure — one rule for us and another for everyone else — which is precisely the shadow the Banknote's G carries. Its figures are David in the archetypal set, whose loyalty to his own house outlives his own justice; Pope Alexander VI in the historical, who made nepotism an instrument of office; Bellatrix Lestrange in the modern, devotion with no object but the master. Every fallen direction on this wheel is the same virtue continued rather than reversed, which is the wheel's central claim about character. "If ye love them which love you, what thank have ye?" (Luke 6:32).

Patronage is the combination of Loyalty and Dignity: a bond honored from a position of strength. The wheel blends its colors by nature rather than by doctrine — orange is the child of the yellow and the red that flank it — and the seat is the Cube's Steady Guardian read flat. Its figures are Boaz in the archetypal set, who redeems a claim he was not obliged to redeem; Lorenzo de' Medici in the historical, whose household made a century of art possible; Charles Xavier in the modern, who shelters and raises his own kind. Patronage answers a permanent question of the two rosters: what a person with weight does with people who have none. "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" (Proverbs 17:17).

Favoritism is Patronage past its measure: the patron's weight spent on the bond instead of on the work. It marks the exact point at which raising your own becomes preferring your own, and the wheel places it beside Tribalism because the two falls differ only in whether the partial party has power to distribute. Its figures are King Lear in the archetypal set, who divides a kingdom by declarations of love; Nicolae Ceaușescu in the historical, whose state became a household; Denethor II in the modern, who weighs two sons and says which he would rather have kept. "Ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing... are ye not then partial in yourselves?" (James 2:3-4).

Dignity is the positive pole of the Self-Regard axis: the correct estimate of one's own worth, held without apology. The Character wheel dresses this horizontal in the Scale's own colors rather than in the Cube's, because the axis IS the scale of self the dial has always drawn — Judas' midnight blue against Lucifer's ember red. Its figures are King Arthur in the archetypal set, Nelson Mandela in the historical and T'Challa in the modern: three whose authority is worn as an office rather than owned as a possession. The Banknote's M holds the same seal, mastery rightly borne — "well done, good and faithful servant... ruler over many things" (Matthew 25:21). "Strength and honour are her clothing" (Proverbs 31:25).

Self-Worship is Dignity continued until the office and the man are confused. It is the oldest fall on this dial and the only one recorded as a first-person ambition: "I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God" (Isaiah 14:13). Its figures are Lucifer in the archetypal set, Salvador Dalí in the historical and Lord Voldemort in the modern. Its true diagonal is Humility directly across the wheel — the same axis the Prism reads as Judas against Lucifer and the Cube reads as Self-Regard, here drawn as one straight line.

Conviction is the combination of Integrity and Dignity: a principle held with enough self-worth to stand on it alone. Pink is red thinned by the moonlight of the pole beside it — the wheel blends by light, exactly as green and orange are blended by nature — and the seat is the Cube's Wise Statesman read flat. Its figures are Elijah in the archetypal set, alone against the prophets of Baal; Martin Luther in the historical, whose "Here I stand, I can do no other" is the seat's own sentence; Steve Rogers in the modern, whose refusals are always addressed to his own side. Conviction is distinguished from stubbornness by sequence: the principle exists before the stand, not because of it. "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind" (Romans 14:5).

Dogmatism is Conviction past its measure: the principle kept after it has stopped being examined. It is the Legalism of the Judgment axis crossed with the pride of the Self-Regard axis — the rule held because holding it has become an identity. Its figures are Creon in the archetypal set, whose edict outlives its reason; Joseph Stalin in the historical, who made doctrine an instrument of arithmetic; Dolores Umbridge in the modern, cruelty administered strictly by the regulation. "The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life" (2 Corinthians 3:6).

Integrity is the negative pole of the Judgment axis: judgment that rests on principle rather than on bonds. Its hue is the moon-gray violet the Rose keeps and never royal purple — the color of midnight, of the Moon and of the Winter Solstice — and the Banknote seats Omega here, the letter of the end: "one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law" (Matthew 5:18). Its figures are Abraham in the archetypal set, Socrates in the historical and Batman in the modern: three who accept a cost rather than make an exception. Set directly opposite Loyalty, it states the wheel's basic disagreement about what a judgment may rest on. "He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not" (Psalm 15:4).

Legalism is Integrity walked past its measure: the law kept until it consumes the reason it was written for. It is the fall this dial argues against most often, because it is the only fall that can be performed without committing a single vice. Its figures are Inspector Javert in the archetypal set, who cannot survive an exception; Maximilien Robespierre in the historical, virtue administered by statute; Judge Dredd in the modern, the office and the code merged into one body. The cure is not less principle but the opposite pole's own gift, a bond the rule must answer to. "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27).

Renunciation is the combination of Integrity and Humility: a principle held by someone who does not need to be its beneficiary. Cyan is blue thinned by the moonlight of the pole beside it, and the seat is the Cube's Contemplative Sage read flat. Its figures are John the Baptist in the archetypal set, whose "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30) is the seat's own sentence; Thomas More in the historical, who resigned an office rather than sign; Obi-Wan Kenobi in the modern, who trains a successor and steps out of the way. Renunciation is the deliberate subtraction of self from a cause one goes on serving. "Whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple" (Luke 14:33).

Mortification is Renunciation past its measure: subtraction continued after there is nothing left to subtract from. Discipline becomes its own object, and the wheel seats it beside Legalism because both are rules that have outlived their purpose — one applied outward, one inward. Its figures are Father Ferapont in the archetypal set, whose fasting is the vanity it claims to kill; Simone Weil in the historical, whose refusal of food outran the solidarity it was meant to express; Silas in the modern, obedience measured in wounds. "Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body" (Colossians 2:23).

Humility is the negative pole of the Self-Regard axis: the correct estimate of one's own worth, held downward. It is accuracy and not self-contempt — the Prism already reads this arm as the descent chosen on purpose, the exact counterweight to Lucifer's climb. Its figures are Jesus Christ in the archetypal set, Mahatma Gandhi in the historical and Superman in the modern: three whose power is larger than their claim on it. Blue is the Scale's own midnight, and the horizontal it anchors — Humility against Dignity — is the axis this canon has always read as the scale of self. "He that humbleth himself shall be exalted" (Luke 14:11).

Self-Annihilation is Humility continued past the point where a self remains to be humble. Its figures are Judas Iscariot in the archetypal set, Franz Kafka in the historical and Darth Vader in the modern: three who concluded that the correct estimate of their own worth was zero. Judas wears two colors on this dial and both are argued — blue is his night, the kiss in the dark and the Scale's own midnight window; green is his fall, humility inverted. The Banknote names the shadow exactly: the grain that dies without bringing forth fruit (John 12:24).

Devotion is the combination of Loyalty and Humility: a bond served from below. Green is the child of the blue and the yellow that flank it — the wheel blends by nature, as the Prism does — and the seat is the Cube's Quiet Devotee read flat. Its figures are Moses in the archetypal set, who intercedes for a people that has just disowned him; Janusz Korczak in the historical, who went with the children he could have left; Alfred Pennyworth in the modern, a lifetime of service that never once asks for the name on the door. Devotion is what Loyalty becomes when the loyal party has nothing to gain in rank. "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends" (John 15:13).

Martyrdom on this wheel is Devotion past its measure: the self spent on the bond until the spending has become the point. The term is used strictly here — not death suffered for a truth, but destruction sought as the proof of an attachment. Its figures are Samson in the archetypal set, who pulls the house down with himself inside it; Marcus Antonius in the historical, an empire traded for an attachment; Severus Snape in the modern, a life administered entirely as penance for one. Its cure is the opposite pole's own gift: enough self-worth for the bond to be served by a living servant. "Though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing" (1 Corinthians 13:3).

The Quiet Devotee is the cube corner where Composure, Loyalty and Humility meet: a bond kept without haste and without a claim attached to it. It is the only vertex whose three axes all point away from the self at once, which is why its work is almost never visible while it is being done. Its DEEDS hold the seat, not its persons. Mary answers the annunciation with a consent that asks for nothing in return — the whole act is one sentence and no condition. Florence Nightingale is seated by the return itself: the most celebrated woman in England came home from Scutari in August 1856 under a false name, on an ordinary boat, and walked into her mother's house unannounced — the welcome the country had prepared for her simply declined, in the one moment where it could not have been refused politely. (Her mortality statistics are the greater work, and they argue the Reformer's seat at 06h rather than this one.) Faramir's is a single refusal — he lets the Ring walk out of Ithilien, declining what his brother reached for, and reports it to no one as a virtue. Yellow crowns the seat because a covenant kept quietly is the oldest form judgment takes. "Be it unto me according to thy word" (Luke 1:38).
